Linear regression techniques, particularly those used in high-dimensional data such as factor analysis and PCA regression, can be utilized to determine which variables contribute to an outcome in an observational study by estimating their relative importance. By applying these methods, researchers can identify key variables that are influential in explaining the outcome and use this information to guide the design of observational studies, focusing resources on the most relevant variables. We investigated the effectiveness of this method in identifying both well-balanced causal variables and those that correlate with confounders, as well as its sensitivity to variables influenced by the treatment but determined by confounder-covariation. Through simulation studies, we demonstrated that our proposed approach can pinpoint balanced causal variables while reducing the risk of selecting variables that correlate with confounders, especially when sample sizes are large. We also examined this method in real-world data from the NHANES study to identify variables that correlate with body mass index and variables that correlate with confounders, particularly those influenced by socioeconomic status.

This study explores the concept of "smart grids" and their interaction with voltage source converters (VSCs), which are crucial for managing power system oscillations by controlling coherency and participation factors. To achieve this, a novel control approach is developed using the dynamic model of the classical participation factor. The effectiveness of this control scheme is tested through a simulation-based approach, which also considers the impact of communication constraints and time delays on the control system's performance. The results of the simulations demonstrate the scheme's ability to regulate power system oscillations over an interconnected network.

We investigate the evolution of a single photon emitted from an atomic ensemble with two atoms having different decay rates. This setup yields a photon with dual characteristics: it emits light that exhibits correlated, coherent properties while also displaying incoherent light due to the distinct decay times of its emitting atoms. This peculiar behavior is further analyzed in the context of the single-photon subspace, where the emitted light's evolution is described by an effective Hamiltonian. Our analysis also explores the impact of the initial atomic coherence on the single photon's properties and presents a potential experimental realization using a multi-level alkali atom with two distinct transitions.

The study of kink models that have internal modes reveals that including these modes can lead to a reduction in kink stability, with the most unstable mode identifying the kink profile. This internal mode effect is most pronounced when the external mode influence is minimal. By examining the kink profile, it is possible to determine the most unstable mode and thereby identify the most critical internal mode contributing to kink stability, while the remainder of the modes have a negligible effect. This approach is applied to the $\varphi^4$ theory and the $\phi^4$ cubic non-linear Schrödinger model.

We have developed a theoretical framework to link generalized parton distributions (GPDs) to the production of hadrons and final-state interaction effects in electron-scattering experiments. Within our approach, the GPDs' quark component is calculated using an unquenched model that combines constituent quarks and dynamical gluons, while sea and light quark effects are modelled as short-range correlations. By accounting for these correlations, our framework accurately reproduces measured values for the proton's $F_2$ structure function and the helicity structure functions $g_1^p$ and $g_1^n$. Furthermore, our model predicts the GPDs' dependence on the longitudinal momentum transfer, and we have calculated the GPDs' sea quark components for the pion, which we compare to existing data.

Text classification research has traditionally relied on standard optimizers and has not thoroughly examined the effects of noise on classification models. In this study, we investigate the impact of discrete noise on text classification tasks and discover that the decision boundary of a trained model is significantly affected by the noise added, which in turn leads to the model forgetting certain training examples. Our findings indicate that introducing discrete noise helps to prevent the model from forgetting information and forgetting rates can be controlled by adjusting the probability of noise addition, thereby enhancing the model's robustness and generalizability to new, unseen data.

A growing interest in computer-assisted polyp detection using endoscopic video has led researchers to explore the application of deep learning techniques for polyp segmentation. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in polyp segmentation, but they have faced challenges in feature aggregation and information utilization from the video. To address this issue, we introduce a novel channel-aware attention (CAAtten) module that leverages temporal information to enhance feature extraction and fusion in video processing. By implementing CAAtten in our proposed deep learning network, we achieve improved polyp segmentation results, yielding a high Dice score of 0.8958, a low mean absolute error (MAE) of 10.84 pixels, and a fast processing speed of 70 ms on the Kvasir-Train and Kvasir-Test datasets.

We've developed a straightforward yet efficient approach to creating complex networks that mimic key characteristics. This method involves starting with an existing network and systematically selecting new nodes based on their ties with existing nodes. By adjusting the spreading factor thatgoverns this process, we can produce network ensembles that exhibit varying degrees of diversity. Notably, our method enables the generation of ensembles with an extensive range of parameters, outperforming conventional methods like the Infomap algorithm. Furthermore, our approach allows for the incorporation of user-defined functions to tailor the spreading function to specific network types.

During $rp$-process-driven Type-I X-ray bursts, the nuclear network is disrupted by bypassing specific waiting points, including $^{56}$Ni. Our research on this phenomenon in Type-I X-ray bursts within $1.7$ and $2.0\, M_{\odot}$ O-Ne white dwarfs reveals that $^{56}$Ni is consistently bypassed in $>70\%$ of all bursts, but its actual impact on $rp$-process yields depends on the specific nuclear processing involved. We discovered that $^{56}$Ni bypassing can lead to the creation of $^{61}$Cu through $3\alpha$ reactions, but this outcome is highly dependent on the specific nuclear processing involved. We also found that $r$-process outcomes are influenced by the specific nuclear processing involved, but they can still produce a wide variety of heavy elements, including rare elements such as $^{198}$Hg, $^{207}$Pb, and $^{209}$Bi, among others. Our research also suggests that $r$-process-driven Type-I X-ray bursts can produce $^{208}$Rn, $^{207}$Hg, and $^{207}$Tl, but these outcomes are highly dependent on the specific nuclear processing involved. Our findings indicate that $r$-process-driven Type-I X-ray bursts can produce a wide variety of heavy elements, including rare elements, but further research is needed to understand the

In the initial section, we demonstrate that components of the flat portion of the Satake locus coincide with cosets of torsion for specific abelian models, particularly those of semi-abelian varieties. Furthermore, we prove that the flat part's components are the largest possible cosets of torsion in these models. In the subsequent section, we establish that the Satake locus's flat portion is the largest part of the whole locus, with the non-flat portion being a collection of smaller torsion cosets. In an appendix by Taylor, we find that the Satake locus's flat portion can be expressed as the intersection of abelian locus components, each translated by a rational point on a model of the given abelian variety.

A comprehensive review of observations made by the MAGIC observatory for nearly two decades is provided, covering various aspects of its performance and scientific research. This review includes an update on the state of the instrument, an overview of significant advancements in its capabilities, an in-depth examination of key scientific achievements and challenges, and an assessment of future prospects. A particular emphasis is placed on the impact of High Frequency and Very High Energy gamma-ray observations on our understanding of astrophysical sources of gamma-ray emission.

This research examines a range of nonlocal boundary-distributed elliptic equations, yielding an existence and uniqueness proof for strong solutions in bounded domains and establishing a $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity analysis for such solutions in the context of smooth domain geometries.

We utilized the Gaia DR3 catalog, featuring 2.5 million stars with 6-color photometry, to classify compact stellar systems in the Milky Way. By applying a supervised machine learning model trained on known globular and ultra-compact dwarf clusters, we were able to classify the stellar systems with an accuracy exceeding 80% when using all available colors. The results indicated that $bp-rp$ and $gr/rp$, specifically, provide the most valuable information for classification. When these three colors were used, the accuracy reached 88%. By employing a novel approach to identify the most informative colors, we were able to classify the stellar systems with an accuracy exceeding 83% using just two colors. The classification was then applied to the stellar systems in the Sloan-Gaia plane, resulting in the identification of 19 possible globular clusters, 7 possible ultra-compact dwarf clusters, and 10 possible core-collapse globular clusters. The classification was also used to analyze the stellar systems in the Galactic Center, resulting in the identification of 6 possible globular clusters, 2 possible ultra-compact dwarf clusters, and 1 possible core-collapse globular cluster.

The use of simulations in building Recommender Systems is a relatively underdeveloped area of study. Although simulations are widely employed in other fields to enhance understanding and experimentation, their potential benefits for RS design are yet to be fully realized. This study explores the possibilities of simulations in RS construction by highlighting their versatility and practical applications. A framework is introduced to demonstrate the synergy between simulations and RS, and three innovative approaches are presented. Through a combination of theoretical and practical insights, the significance of simulations in RS construction is further elucidated.

We investigate testing hypotheses for infinite parameters in infinite mean or variance distributions using truncated sample means. The proposed test statistic does not require knowledge of the underlying distribution, except for its finite moment conditions. The test's validity and consistency are established under these conditions. Furthermore, the rate of convergence of the test is demonstrated to be $\sqrt{n/\log n}$, where $n$ represents the sample size.

Recent advancements in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have led to their successful application in various tasks within the field of Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs). However, the application of CNNs in brain signal processing, specifically EEG, is hindered by the problems of limited data availability and the high computational demands required for training these models. To address these issues, we have developed a novel framework that leverages the capabilities of CNNs and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithms. By employing a data augmentation technique that utilizes the internal knowledge of the MCTS algorithm, our proposed framework can effectively learn from the analysis of simulated data, thereby enhancing the generalization of the CNNs. Furthermore, the use of MCTS allows for the efficient sampling of data, thereby reducing the computational costs associated with training CNNs. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we have developed a novel BCI-based system for controlling a mobile robot's trajectory using EEG signals. The results of our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach in terms of its ability to generalize to unseen data, with an average of 85% accuracy in predicting motor imagery (MI) events, and a response time of approximately 2.5 seconds.

The AdS/CFT correspondence has been successfully applied to scalar fields on a noncommutative, asymptotically AdS_5 space, and in this study, we have explored the noncommutative properties of these fields.  Using the classical equations of motion, we have derived a set of equations that describe massive scalar fields in a noncommutative environment, and we have identified the corresponding holographic duals for such fields.  We have also established a relationship between the noncommutative scalar fluctuations and the properties of a type IIB string in a deformed background.  By analyzing the noncommutative fluctuations in this context, we have been able to determine the properties of a deformed background, and our results are consistent with those obtained from the classical equations of motion.  These findings open up new possibilities for applying the AdS/CFT correspondence to noncommutative spaces, and we believe that they will contribute to a greater understanding of the relationship between noncommutative properties and the geometry of spacetime at a holographic level.

In kidney transplantations, patients with kidney disease are often in need of a compatible organ donor. However, due to various genetic factors, finding a compatible donor is challenging, and patients may receive a kidney from an incompatible donor following a pre-transplant desensitization process. This process involves undergoing various treatments, such as plasmapheresis, to make the donor kidney compatible, and as a result, patients may experience a decrease in their quality of life. This decrease can be represented by an "incompatibility" variable in a Markov Decision Process model, allowing for the analysis of when it is optimal to undergo desensitization and receive a transplant from an incompatible donor. In fact, incorporating this variable into the model allows for a 35% reduction in desensitization attempts while still maximizing the discounted utility, indicating its importance in decision-making.

This research examines the hidden state structures of two popular neural network models, Hidden Markov Models and Long Short-Term Memory Models, with a focus on their expressiveness and generalization capabilities. We develop a framework to analyze and compare these models and their associated learning algorithms. Our investigation reveals that while Hidden Markov Models possess comparable expressiveness to Long Short-Term Memory Models, they exhibit significantly reduced generalization performance across a range of benchmark datasets. This discrepancy highlights the need for more effective evaluation methods in machine learning.

This research focuses on operator classifications related to weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, providing new descriptions of operator properties such as compactness, boundedness, and being of Schatten class. The study utilizes a novel method involving equivalent operator spaces in the p-Bergman space, defined relative to a specific finite measure on the unit disk. This approach leads to simplified expressions for key operator characteristics and supports the derivation of several new theorems regarding operator space isomorphism.

This research investigates the application of compressed neural networks to automatic keyword extraction from scientific texts. The aim is to develop highly efficient models for indoor climate monitoring, specifically in building and infrastructure monitoring. The effectiveness of model compression methods on this task is evaluated, focusing on their impact on compression ratio, accuracy, and model performance. The performance of compressed models is assessed using the accuracy of a downstream task - a text-based classification of monitoring data. The findings reveal that certain compression methods significantly improve model efficiency without compromising classification accuracy.

In the 2014 Winter Convening of the USPAS, a new concept in software development was proposed as a valuable contribution to the field of High Energy Physics: Scientific Machine to Machine (M2M) Communication.  This innovative approach facilitates the exchange of data and tools between complex computing systems, offering versatility and ease of use.  The design of a user-friendly interface and associated capabilities were demonstrated through the implementation of a Monte Carlo generator for ATLAS detector simulations at the Large Hadron Collider.

We define a generalized form of Howe curves, incorporating parameters from the isomorphism of abelian surfaces and demonstrating their relationship with a specific decomposition of Richelot isogenies. We further establish a method for their systematic construction and examine some of their inherent properties.

A recent study has identified 63 magnetic hot subdwarfs, which include 41 newly classified stars, that exhibit strong magnetic fields. The study analyzed these stars using a combination of photometric data, spectroscopy, and modeling. The results revealed that 41 of these stars are new discoveries, which have been confirmed through spectroscopic and photometric observations. The study also found that 41 of these 63 magnetic hot subdwarfs are He-white dwarf binaries, and 33 of them have been identified as helium-white dwarf binaries for the first time. The study has provided the first detailed analysis of helium-white dwarf binaries, and the results have been used to study the evolution of helium-white dwarf binaries, the mass transfer process, and the magnetic fields of these stars. The study has also found that the hydrogen abundances in these stars do not match the current model predictions, which may indicate that the stars have undergone changes in hydrogen abundance during their evolution. The study has also identified 5 stars that are likely to be single objects with extremely strong magnetic fields, and the results have been used to study the properties of these stars.

We use invariant matrix theory to investigate errors in approximating matrices, focusing on specific low-rank tensor structures. This approach leads to new, simpler matrix rank conditions for low-rank tensor approximations. The theory also helps clarify the relationship between different low-rank tensor models, such as PARAFAC and Tucker, and their generalization, CP- Tucker. We apply this understanding to approximate tensor decompositions, and by analyzing the subspaces within these tensors, we establish new relationships between Tucker and PARAFAC decompositions.

This research examines the role of hyperlinks in Wikipedia's editing process through comparative analyses of HTML and wikitext.  Hyperlinks in HTML serve to connect to other Wikipedia articles, whereas those in wikitext serve a dual purpose, facilitating a link to other articles while also providing a summary or introduction to those articles.  This distinction enables identification of potential modifications to articles during the review process.  Our analysis of data from 2019 reveals that, although both HTML and wikitext often introduce new articles, HTML tend to focus on more localized modifications, whereas wikitext tend to involve broader overviews, and that editors using HTML are more likely to make substantial changes.

Recent research has shown that twisted bilayers of graphene exhibit polar domains with distinct electronic and topological characteristics. These properties are now being explored in a range of materials systems. This work provides a unified framework for understanding the electronic properties of twisted bilayers, unifying the study of single and multiple layers. By applying a simple model, the properties of these systems can be explained and their unique polar domain structure can be leveraged to advance topological physics and related technologies, including those involving superconductivity and quantum transport.

The trajectory of a light beam in a universe with non-flat geometry differs significantly from that in a flat universe. As a result, the trajectory of a photon from an emission point to a reception point in non-flat space can intersect itself, and the number of self-intersections depends on changes in the universe's expansion rate between the emission and reception events. We find that self-intersections occur in both expanding and contracting universes, and demonstrate that space-time topological features, such as the number of self-intersections, can be influenced by observations, such as supernovae and gravitational lensing.

We investigated how a colloidal particle moves in a nematic liquid crystal confined between two parallel walls, with one wall having alternating patterns of high and low ridges. By analyzing the interaction between the particle and the liquid crystal using a simplified model, we found that the particle's trajectory depends significantly on its size relative to the spacing between the ridges. At small particle sizes, it behaves similarly to the system with smooth walls, while at large sizes, it follows periodic orbits that are determined by the strength of the liquid crystal and the spacing between the ridges. We observed that the particle can remain in a stable position against the liquid crystal flows, provided that it is positioned in the valleys of the ridges.

The tidal effects caused by a nearby body in an asteroid's evolution have been a topic of interest. However, the elongation of an asteroid has been seen as a factor that only affects the system when it exceeds the Roche limit, but this perspective is too narrow. In reality, the tidal forces exerted by a nearby body on an asteroid's equatorial equilibration time scale indicate that even before reaching the Roche limit, the asteroid's shape and orientation will experience the effects of tidal forces. Furthermore, the equilibration time scale of an asteroid's shape under these conditions reveals that the tidal forces can persist for a considerable amount of time, often longer than the timescales associated with other dynamical effects.

The integration of machine learning and quantum computing has opened up new avenues for advancing molecular dynamics simulations. A particular challenge in this field is analyzing rare and significant molecular transformations that occur infrequently. Due to these events' scarcity, traditional sampling methods often fail to capture them. Leveraging the benefits of both machine learning and quantum computing, we have developed an innovative approach to identify and study these rare transformations. Our algorithm, which relies on machine learning to detect significant structural changes and a quantum algorithm to simulate the subsequent molecular dynamics, has been shown to be highly effective. When applied to the alanine dipeptide molecule, which is known for exhibiting complex and time-consuming conformational changes, our approach successfully identified and characterized the molecule's dominant transformation. Our findings demonstrate the potential of combining machine learning and quantum computing to study rare molecular changes and we believe this method will have significant implications for understanding complex biochemical processes.

We introduce MAPPIES, a Monte Carlo code for simulating polarisation in X-ray and gamma-ray emissions resulting from inverse Compton scattering and synchrotron radiation. This code is designed to run on a GPU, allowing for rapid simulations of high-resolution light curves and polarisation images. Developed using CUDA and CUDA's automatic parallelisation, MAPPIES runs efficiently on a graphics card. We demonstrate its capabilities by simulating polarisation in the Crab Nebula's X-ray spectrum and its potential applications in future polarimetry missions.

To better understand the role of open water in sea-ice formation, we conducted a detailed analysis of the Met Office's Sea Ice Model (SAM code). We investigated the effects of open water on the evolution of sea ice in the Arctic Ocean, focusing on a specific region, and found that the introduction of open water accelerates the decline of thick sea ice categories. This, in turn, affects the distribution of ice types in the region, with an increase in thin ice and a decrease in old ice. These changes have significant implications for the production of real sea ice observations from satellite imagery. The research revealed that the current method used to create fake sea ice is not sufficient to accurately capture the differences between open and closed sea-ice conditions, particularly in relation to thin ice areas. Therefore, we developed a new approach that effectively distinguishes between open and closed sea-ice conditions, even when the ice is young and smooth. The research outcomes will be integrated into the Met Office's operational ice production system to ensure that it can accurately identify open water from satellite imagery.

In this paper, we explore the families of curves $\mathfrak{X}_{a,b,n,s}$ and $\mathfrak{Y}_{n,s}$, where $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime, to understand their coverage by Hermitian curves. We find that these families are unique in that they can be covered by Hermitian curves but cannot be covered by non-Hermitian curves. We also establish a connection between the curves $\mathfrak{X}_{a,b,n,s}$ and the rational curves with singular points on the Kummer model, as well as those on the projective line with certain multiplicity conditions. Finally, we consider the miminal degree needed to cover these families and provide a solution for specific cases involving the families $\mathfrak{X}_{1,1,n,s}$ and $\mathfrak{X}_{1,2,n,s}$.

Voice synthesis technology has advanced significantly for non-singing voices, but synthesizing high-quality singing voices remains a challenge for both commercial use and academic research, largely due to the scarcity of extensive singing datasets. To address this issue, we present a massive new dataset for singing voice synthesis, compiled from over 1,500 hours of audio and video recordings of over 150,000 minutes. This dataset contains a rich variety of audio and video information, including speech, singing, and hybrid content, along with detailed alignments and annotations for multiple aspects. To further enhance the dataset's utility, we provide a range of annotation and extraction tools, enabling the separation of different audio elements. This dataset aims to facilitate advancements in singing voice synthesis and related tasks, such as singing voice identification and separation.

We introduce NIPS4Bplus, a cutting-edge dataset that consists of ecoacoustic recordings collected from four European rivers over two years. The dataset includes annotated bird and whale vocalizations, as well as background noise, and was captured using specialized riverfloaters equipped with hydrodynamic sensors and custom-designed acoustic units. The dataset is accessible, and we outline potential applications for NIPS4Bplus in advancing ecoacoustic research and monitoring, including mitigating the impacts of riverine noise and aiding marine biodiversity monitoring efforts.

We introduce a straightforward approach for calibrating event cameras in a coordinate system based on frame data from other image sources. This method enables the transformation of event camera coordinates to frame-based coordinates. In contrast to previous approaches, we utilize an event intensity image to achieve extrinsic alignment without requiring the estimation of spatial and temporal sensor characteristics. This transformation is achieved through a learning-based network trained on ground truth data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world datasets, resulting in accurate and efficient alignment between event and frame data.

Graph learning techniques have been successfully applied in various domains beyond social and e-commerce networks, such as predicting disease progression from medical records and analyzing gene expression to identify cancer subtypes. These models rely on graph representations learned through neural networks and can be trained using node embeddings developed via random walks through the graph. However, the widespread use of graph learning has not yet led to a deeper understanding of how these models actually work. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted an experiment that examined the impact of different walk strategies on model performance. Our results show that the effectiveness of these models often stems not from the specific sequence in which the walk samples are taken, but rather from the diversity of the sequences themselves. This discovery suggests that future improvements in graph learning may focus on incorporating more varied sequences of sampling.

Using the braid group on 4 strands, we develop a method to create new exceptional collections on $\Bbb P^1 \times \Bbb P^1$, specifically on the Hirzebruch surface of degree 2, and discover their connections to derived equivalences between derived categories of $\Bbb P^1 \times \Bbb P^1$ and $\Bbb P^1 \times \Bbb P^1 \times \Bbb P^1$.

Retinal surgeons encounter numerous challenges when operating in 3D environments, with a key issue being the limited, two-dimensional perspective offered by the eye's natural lens. To overcome this, we've developed a cutting-edge, AI-powered system that employs a cutting method to guide retinal surgeons. Our innovative'spotlight' projection technique enhances 3D guidance by mimicking the way the human eye processes images to spot abnormalities. By projecting this projection onto the original 3D image, we've found that our method significantly outperforms conventional approaches in detecting retinal problems in 2D images.

Building on a previously established product formula, we can express the $F$-polynomial of a closure graph as the sum of $F$-polynomials of its closure line graphs. We demonstrate that this sum can be broken down further into a linear combination of the same collection of line graph $F$-polynomials.

The introduction of FIDO2 by the World Wide Web Consortium as an open standard has paved the way for a password-free authentication experience. FIDO2 enables users to interact with a secure chip on their devices to authenticate through various methods. This chapter delves into the technical aspects underlying FIDO2 and explains the specifications outlined in SPML v2.0, PIN, Credential Management, and Public Key algorithms, as well as the security measures implemented in FIDO2. Furthermore, the development of FIDO2 is also discussed, including its progression, adoption, and integration with existing systems, along with the potential future directions for FIDO2.

A novel Weyl-Wigner formalism, grounded in a deformed Moyal bracket, has been developed. The primary objective was to apply this framework to quantum physics involving qubits. Nonetheless, the algebraic intricacies associated with qubit-based systems proved to be the limiting factors, rendering it challenging to apply this approach to these specific quantum systems. The underlying issues with the deformed Weyl-Wigner formalism were also investigated, which may indicate that it is more suitable for studying continuous variable theories. The outcomes of this work are likely to contribute to ongoing research in this area.

A fundamental aspect of user experience in video apps is the ability to influence
how content is presented. The majority of these apps utilize a combination of
controls, such as buttons and swipes, to empower users and provide a sense of
control. Our study, a first of its kind, examines the role of user interfaces in
video apps by focusing on the impact of a time delay in streaming. This
innovative approach allows us to explore new ways of interacting with
applications and understanding the significance of control within the context
of video consumption. Our research involved conducting interviews with 13 experts
from the field of video apps and conducting a co-design workshop with 5 users.
Our initial analysis revealed the significance of certain controls, such as
buttons and swipes, in regulating the viewing experience. Our experiment,
which involved providing the participants with a time delay in streaming, gave
us valuable insights into their preferences and needs. Our study has identified
several areas for improvement in video apps and provides recommendations for
future development.

We demonstrate that the π-calculus cannot specify behaviours that are not realizable in a finitely executable manner, as established by a reduction to a fundamental problem for multiset rewriting, which is equivalent to the Turing machines' coverage in specifying all possible computations. A similar outcome is found when examining the reactive version of Turing machines, as a reduction to its equivalent problem for multiset rewriting shows that the reactive version cannot specify behaviours that are not finitely executable either. A detailed proof is provided using a proof search procedure, which is implemented in the unification-theory-of-terms framework, thus making it a fully automated proof. This method has potential applications in other context-free specification languages, such as rewrite systems, graph rewriting and process algebra languages, as it offers a unified framework for proving termination of reductions in different systems.

A unique binary Gray code is developed for ordered trees, enabling a step-by-step transformation from one tree to another without flipping bits at adjacent levels, but rather at levels that are distance $\ell$ apart, where $\ell$ is a constant related to the tree class, thus allowing a faster and more controlled algorithmic search among ordered trees, particularly in tree pattern matching problems.

The process of track reconstruction in heavy ion collision events is complex
primarily due to the high density of secondary particles produced in these
collisions, which results in a high rate of fake links between particles.
To mitigate this issue, the ALICE experiment's track reconstruction algorithm
employs a pattern recognition module that applies constraints based on space
point discrepancies and link topology between patterns. This approach enables
the detection of fake links, which are subsequently discarded in favor of the
remaining patterns. In this study, the performance of this track reconstruction
module is thoroughly evaluated using simulated events across a broad range of
pantile events and verified against actual data from specific events.

A new numerical approach, the time-discontinuous prismatic space-time (D-PST) finite-element method, has been developed to simulate fluid flows with free surfaces. This technique combines a unique space-time formulation, utilizing a prismatic space-time domain, with a time-discontinuous approach. This allows for the use of finite elements in the space direction while maintaining flexibility in the time dimension. This formulation is particularly well-suited for modeling complex free-surface flows, such as those occurring in river and ocean systems, by treating the free surface as part of the computational domain. This method can be used to simulate a variety of fluid dynamics problems, including those governed by the shallow water equations in multiple space dimensions. This study presents a detailed derivation of the D-PST method, a new implementation strategy, and a set of algorithms for simulating such problems. It also explores the impact of numerical dissipation on the method and provides a detailed analysis of the resulting numerical scheme. Finally, the performance of the D-PST method is validated through a series of benchmark tests, including a 1D dam break test, a 1D tidal test, a 1D wave test, a 2D dam break test, and a 2D wave test.

We have developed an algorithm that efficiently creates a circular flow based on a given orientation, where the algorithm's running time is directly proportional to the number of components and the maximum value of k, provided that the graph in question is a specific type of graph denoted as (G,r). This discovery has led to the creation of an algorithm that can efficiently determine if a particular graph orientation has a corresponding circular flow based on a given number, with the algorithm's running time also dependent on the number of components and the maximum value of k, provided that the graph in question is a specific type of graph denoted as (G,r). Additionally, we have found that the existence of a particular flow based on a given number in a specific type of graph is equivalent to the existence of a particular orientation on that graph, which can be used to create a corresponding flow based on a related number in a related graph. This has led to a proof that for a particular number, the number of possible orientations on a given graph is equal to the number of possible corresponding flow pairs for that graph, to the given number.

We investigate the Modular Subset Sum problem, which is defined as: given a set of integers between 0 and $N$, a target number $T$, and an integer $M$, find a subset of integers such that the sum of its elements equals $T$ modulo $M$. A previously developed probabilistic algorithm for this problem had an expected time complexity of $O(N/\text{NCRT})$. In contrast, we present a new, deterministic algorithm that runs in $O(N/\text{NCT})$ time. This new algorithm is based on a technique that allows us to transform the problem into a different instance of Modular Subset Sum with a smaller $N$. This transformation is performed by removing specific elements from the original problem instance. We also introduce a new approach for constructing a dynamic data structure that can be used to find the elements of a subset with a given sum modulo $M$ in $O(\log^2 N)$ time. This new approach is more efficient than previous methods, which required $\Theta(N)$ time. The dynamic data structure is used in conjunction with the algorithm for transforming the problem to achieve the desired time complexity.

Our research involved a comprehensive analysis of 19 M dwarf stars using the 3.6-meter Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. The data collected over 11-16 nights allowed us to identify rotational variables and further categorize them as flaring or non-flaring. We observed a significant difference in rotation period between the two groups, with the flaring group exhibiting shorter periods. We also found that the flaring stars rotate more rapidly, have stronger magnetic fields, and experience more frequent and intense flares. The flares observed in our study varied significantly in amplitude, ranging from 0.5 to 3.5 magnitudes in V-band. The flares lasted anywhere from 10 seconds to 45 minutes, and some stars experienced multiple flares in a single observation. The flares were found to be correlated with the stars' magnetic field strengths and rotation periods. The flares were found to be correlated with the stars' magnetic field strengths and rotation periods. We also found that the flares were influenced by the stars' magnetic field strengths and rotation periods. The laminin receptor LanB1 plays a significant role in the development and function of the fruit fly's immune system. We investigated the role of LanB1 and its mutants SCAR in the movement of fly hemocytes by studying the interaction between LanB1 and Laminin-10 using an in vitro assay. Our results showed that hemocytes lacking LanB1 were unable to move on their own, but when paired with Laminin-10 they moved rapidly. In contrast, flies lacking both LanB1 and SCAR had reduced hemocyte movement compared to those lacking only LanB1, suggesting SCAR's involvement in hemocyte motility. Introducing LanB1 in flies lacking SCAR restored normal movement in the hemocytes. We also observed that hemocytes lacking LanB1 moved more slowly on Laminin-10 over time, but this was not the case for flies lacking SCAR. These findings suggest that LanB1 and SCAR work together to facilitate the movement of fly immune cells within their matrix environment.

We introduce c-siam, an advanced architecture for speech-language correlation, and present SIAM corpora for three language pairs: English-German, English-Spanish, and English-French. c-siam architecture builds upon siam, incorporating a cross-modal attention mechanism that enables more effective linguistic feature extraction. SIAM corpora consist of the same sentence spoken in two languages with separate automatic transcriptions and manual translations. We demonstrate c-siam's ability to accurately predict cross-modal alignment for both matched and mismatched spoken language pairs.

A novel model for describing the interaction between neutrinos and nucleons is developed by applying the parton way of thinking. The model is based on the Baluni-Kilian formula and incorporates the D0-D1-2 collaboration data and GENIE 1.0.00 framework. The updated model exhibits improved alignment with measured neutrino-nucleon total cross-sections and differential data, as well as neutrino-nucleus cross-sections and differential data. The new model provides cross-section predictions across a broad energy range, from 0.1 to $10^{11}$ GeV, thereby enabling predictions for neutrino-nucleus interactions in the GeV and TeV regions, as well as differential properties.

This research paper investigates the almost certain stability of an adaptive control system, where the control process is influenced by hidden Markov chains. We establish that the system is stochastically stable if and only if it satisfies a specific condition in the σ-algebra associated with the Markov chain, using the measurable limit theory of Markov chains to demonstrate this equivalence.

This research introduces a novel approach to text input interpretation, referred to as BTAI, which is designed to facilitate communication between text input and robotic task execution. BTAI's application scope encompasses a range of complex tasks, including those found in domestic settings, manufacturing environments, and hospitals. BTAI's primary function involves converting text input into a structured plan, comprising a set of defined tasks, which can be directly executed by an autonomous robot. BTAI's interpretation framework is based on a Bayesian network, which is trained using a substantial dataset comprising 2,500 text inputs and corresponding robotic tasks. The performance of BTAI is evaluated through a series of experiments involving simulated tasks, which demonstrate that BTAI surpasses its predecessors in terms of efficiency and accuracy. Specifically, experiments demonstrate that BTAI can accurately interpret text inputs approximately 20% more effectively than its predecessors, while also achieving a 2.5-fold improvement in task completion speed.

The sound speed's relationship to the quark gluon plasma's energy density is crucial for obtaining the Korteveg-de Vries equation. Depending on the equation of state, the potential associated with the Korteveg-de Vries equation and its initial condition can either have a symmetric or asymmetric form. A research study found that a particular combination of the radial Hamiltonian and its initial condition generates a solution resembling a quark gluon plasma. Using this solution, the study derived a scaling exponent for the quark gluon plasma and compared it with the one obtained from hydrodynamic scaling relations. A notable finding was that a nonlinear correction to the hydrodynamic scaling relations was necessary to match the numerical results obtained from lattice QCD simulations.

We demonstrate that the space of continuous real-valued functions on a compact space is linearly Eberlein-Grothendick if and only if it lacks a countable network. Consequently, $L_{\infty}([0,1])$ does not possess the Eberlein-Grothendieck property. Furthermore, we establish that any separable Banach space with a countable dense subset has a closed subspace that is linearly Eberlein-Grothendieck. This verifies a conjecture made by Albiac and Gogoladze.

We present a set of conditions for the Taylor series of a single degree of freedom Hamiltonian function that ensures it is isochronous. We also establish relationships between the higher-order coefficients of the Hamiltonian and the phase-dependent coefficients that arise in the rotated frame. We then derive and solve the conditions under which a Hamiltonian remains isochronous when transformed in different coordinate systems, and demonstrate this property for specific potential functions.

Using the local continuation method, various periodic orbits of the Lorenz system are identified and categorized based on their periods. The study of the periodic orbits of the Lorenz system is particularly significant in mathematical biology, as they represent the cycles of heat exchange between the liquid layer and the ambient environment. The research also examines the stability of the periodic orbits, revealing that as the system approaches a critical point, a stable cycle emerges, eventually giving rise to a stable equilibrium. The study further examines the stability of the equilibrium by analyzing the eigenvalues of the system, revealing that one eigenvalue remains constant, while the other two eigenvalues determine the stability of the equilibrium. The research also discovers that the stable cycle gives rise to a pair of unstable spirals and a segment of unstable periodic orbits surrounding it, as the system approaches another critical point. The study also examines the stability of the periodic orbits surrounding the stable cycle, revealing that the stability of the periodic orbits surrounding the stable cycle determines the stability of the system.

This research develops a high-dimensional framework for the Malliavin calculus, enabling the creation of native random elements that are equivalent to a Gaussian process with specified properties. Building upon this, we demonstrate that the Malliavin score, derived from the log-likelihood's derivative, is a viable eligibility criterion for policy gradient optimization in reinforcement learning. Notably, our findings indicate that the Malliavin score can be approximated by a neural network, making it a valuable tool in both offline and online settings. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the Malliavin score in developing diverse policy gradient algorithms and reveal significant performance gains in various reinforcement learning tasks.

We investigate the effect of metric changes on the spectrum of Laplacians in various space-time settings and derive a limit law that describes how critical exponents behave as a metric is transformed through a process called Teichmüller deformation. This generalizes a known result for a specific type of metric change to more complex settings. To achieve this, we first calculate the asymptotic properties of certain geometric functions, then use these results to derive an asymptotic expression for the heat kernel function.

We introduce an innovative autoregressive Fourier transform (AFT), enabling the creation of both efficient and effective time-series prediction models. By leveraging AFT to decompose a given signal into time-dependent Fourier components, we develop a simple, autoregressive model that estimates the inductive bias of a convolutional neural network (CNN). The resulting CNN, equipped with AFT-based components, exhibits improved performance in predicting time-series data from real-world climate and financial datasets, while maintaining fast training times. Furthermore, AFT enables the discovery of predictable time-series patterns using only past data for prediction, without the need for model training.

We examine the connection between the cosmic equation of state parameter and the universe's energy density, as well as other related parameters, in order to assess the compatibility of the $\Lambda$CDM model with observational data. We achieve this by developing a novel method that utilizes a combination of cosmic parameters, integrated into the cosmic equation of state parameter within the $\Lambda$CDM model, as a means to evaluate the compatibility of the data. We apply this approach to a combination of SNIa data, as well as other related parameters, in order to assess the compatibility of the $\Lambda$CDM model with the observational constraints.

To enhance user experience, multi-access edge computing (MEC) employs service function chaining (SFC) for complex applications, but this comes with resource challenges for virtual network functions (VNFs). A new approach, VRF-POA, is proposed to optimize resource allocation for VNFs in MEC. It breaks down the problem into two parts: determining VNF placement and VNF resource allocation. For the first part, VRF-POA uses a branch-and-bound algorithm to find the best placement. For the second part, it uses a column-generation algorithm to find the most efficient resource allocation. Additionally, VRF-POA uses a two-stage algorithm to further optimize resource allocation. Experimental results show that VRF-POA outperforms existing algorithms by up to 26.7% in reducing VNF deployment time and up to 8.2% in reducing VNF resource usage.

We investigate the effects of a $U(1)$ symmetry on a two-dimensional Dirac fermion model with local disorder using the functional renormalization group method. Our findings indicate that as the strength of disorder increases, the fixed point associated with the symmetry becomes increasingly unstable. Furthermore, we analyze the entanglement properties of the system, specifically the thermal entropiness spectrum, and discover that the fixed point associated with the symmetry exhibits characteristics of entanglement entropy that scale logarithmically with the system size.

Recent studies have found that social media data can be utilized to identify individuals who have been diagnosed with depression, demonstrating that patterns in users' online activity and connections can be distinct between those with depression and those without. These studies typically analyze overall trends and differences in how both groups interact with their online environment. However, this study takes a unique approach, focusing on the positive experiences and connections that occur within the online environments of individuals with depression, rather than solely highlighting the differences that exist between these groups. Through this approach, we aim to develop a more comprehensive understanding of how depression manifests in everyday online interactions, rather than solely focusing on the negative or abnormal aspects. To this end, we have developed a new method for identifying the positive experiences and connections that occur within the online environments of individuals with depression, based on a large dataset of over 100,000 Twitter users. Our results show that the positive experiences and connections that occur within the online environments of individuals with depression are significantly lower than those experienced by individuals without depression, but still present in the data. These findings support the idea that depression is not solely defined by negative emotions, but also by a lack of positive experiences and connections.

A QCD-based theory with a light, weakly-interacting gauge boson can serve as a viable dark matter explanation, with the gauge symmetry being a key factor in preventing the gauge boson from mass and stability. A specific example of this concept involves the $SU(6)$ gauge theory, where a given sector is broken at the mass of a few GeV, resulting in the emergence of a dark matter candidate. A thorough analysis of this model has been conducted, with the numerical results indicating that the model is capable of generating the correct abundance of dark matter, aligning with the observed abundance when the gauge coupling is strong.

A new method utilizing in-situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy has been developed to quantify the magnetic ordering temperature, local structure, and crystal field influence on 3d ions in transition metal compounds. The technique was applied to Na$_{4-\delta}$Ni$_{4-\delta}$TeO$_6$, where it identified an unusually large Ni$^{2+}$ spin in a square planar environment, and revealed how the Te-O-Ni-O-Te bond angle and CEF effect on the Ni spin are influenced by the Te-O bond length. The results suggest that the Te-O bond length contracts as the crystal field influence on the Ni spin increases, and that the Ni spin size can be significantly reduced by the CEF effect in this compound, resulting in a substantial reduction of the magnetic ordering temperature.

Decisions made at a central location, like a cloud server, are often met with skepticism in large-scale distributed systems, especially those in the Internet of Things. For such systems to function securely, the entities involved must be trustworthy, a notion evaluated based on the reputation they've built through consistent behavior. This behavior, however, can be compromised by malicious entities aiming to deceive, and even well-intentioned ones may struggle to drive meaningful decision-making with traditional repute systems. This work proposes a new decision framework that leverages the Web3 ecosystem, allowing the integration of decentralized identity standards and the Secure Interprocess Application Programming Interface (SIPA) queue, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a simulation that compares it to existing solutions.

In various fields like engineering and finance, cubic splines with data preservation are crucial for monotonic solutions. This article introduces new methods for direct computation of cubic spline interpolants subject to piecewise linear constraints. It also presents an algorithm for a cubic spline with an additional concavity constraint. A second derivative formula is derived using different techniques for constrained cubic splines. Furthermore, the article showcases applications in time series interpolation and risk management, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

This study examines the AdS black bounce geometry with a scalar field and
quantum scalar field. We analyze the phase changes in the classical and quantum
bounce systems across different AdS spacetime dimensions and scalar potentials.
Our analysis reveals significant differences in the phase transitions of dS and AdS
black bounce configurations. We investigate the stability of dS and AdS black
bounces with a scalar field and quantum scalar field, focusing on the fundamental
properties of the black bounce model.

The growing interest in audio analysis tools has led to an increase in research focused on automated techniques for audio content annotation, particularly through the use of machine learning algorithms. However, traditional methods of manual annotation are often impractical due to difficulties in scaling with the variety and quantity of audio content. This has prompted the development of automatic annotation tools that utilize pre-defined models to identify specific audio events. While these tools have been successful in some cases, they often fail when dealing with more complex tasks such as audio segmentation and labeling. This study aims to address these challenges by introducing a novel method for creating customized segmentation models based on a comprehensive audio dataset. This dataset is used to train a deep learning model that can identify and learn the characteristics of specific audio events. The developed method has been successfully tested on a dataset of music tracks and demonstrated promising results, achieving an accuracy rate of 71.4% in recognizing and classifying individual audio segments.

The dynamics of ecological and biochemical systems are characterized by the coexistence of multiple species, which can be a result of stable equilibrium. However, these systems are also susceptible to instability and the emergence of dominant species that eventually dominate or render others extinct. This phenomenon is analogous to the instability observed in nonequilibrium chemical reactions. Our research examines the stability of systems consisting of multiple species under nonequilibrium conditions, specifically those with limited resources. We found that systems with limited resources exhibit a dual response in terms of stability, with an initial increase in stability followed by a collapse. This collapse is triggered by the emergence of a stable equilibrium where a few species dominate. Notably, the dynamics of ecological systems are similar to those of biochemical reactions, suggesting a common mechanism behind coexistence in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions.

We examine the sequence of fragmentation events in a complex network that occurs as a result of sequential node removal. Utilizing the London Underground map and the World Wide Web as examples, we investigate the process of avalanche progression and explore how the size of individual fragmentation events is influenced by their occurrence. Our findings indicate that the size of these events follows a power-law distribution and that the magnitude of the exponent is contingent upon the initial network configuration.

Developing models that accurately track a speaker's reference within dialogue is a difficult task, crucial for a deeper understanding of discourse as a whole. The challenge lies in the fact that discourse structures are highly flexible and evolve over time, making it hard to create a unified model. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach to learning discourse structures dynamically through self-attention mechanisms. By incorporating a sequence of sequence attention mechanisms, our model effectively builds a dynamic tree structure that organizes discourse in a coherent and layered manner. The model is then able to accurately pinpoint the speaker's reference by utilizing this structured structure. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a thorough evaluation on three benchmark datasets that span both public and private domains, and our results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art systems. The code and models used in this research have been made publicly available for further research and development.

A new approach to absorbing boundary conditions, specifically semi-anisotropic conformal PML, has been developed to efficiently solve seismological problems. This method has been adapted to 2D and 3D models and incorporated into a numerical code. Computational findings indicate that, in comparison to a traditional PML implementation, it can save up to 60% of resources, up to 40% of time, and up to 30% of memory, allowing for significant reductions in computational requirements when solving large-scale seismic inverse problems.

Recent studies have shown that the breakdown of a butterfly in the interaction of two droplets can be explained in terms of a two-stage impact process, where the initial butterfly stage is characterized by a unique pattern of oscillations, and the second stage involves the collapse of this pattern due to a nonlinear effect. This two-stage process was predicted to have a specific pattern of energy distribution, which was observed to match the data obtained from a computer simulation. The analysis also showed that the initial stage contributes more to the overall energy spectrum than the second stage, which is consistent with the data obtained from the computer simulation.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) is driving the need for flexible and efficient network management capabilities. By integrating the control plane and data plane, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) provides the necessary control over network devices and resources. However, the widespread adoption of IoT devices also presents challenges related to data security, specifically in the detection and prevention of advanced malware attacks. In order to address these issues effectively, network operators require a comprehensive understanding of the network traffic and the underlying security processes. In this study, we propose a novel SDN-based security framework that utilizes machine learning and deep learning techniques to identify malware and differentiate between legitimate and suspicious network traffic. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to provide accurate security predictions while maintaining high throughput and minimal latency. Moreover, the framework's adaptability is showcased by its successful deployment in a heterogeneous IoT network consisting of diverse IoT devices and network protocols.

In the early stages of planetary formation, the orbit of a newly created giant planet can be irregular, deviating from a standard circular path.  Such non-planetary orbits may result in a non-uniform structure in the surrounding protoplanetary disk, with the closest areas experiencing the most extreme pressure and temperature fluctuations.  This study examines the effects of a non-circular planet orbit on a protoplanetary disk, with the goal of understanding how the disk's shape and size evolve over time.  Using computer models to simulate the effects of a planet's gravitational pull on the disk, the research team found that the disk's shape and size change significantly over time.  In particular, the disk's density and temperature fluctuations increase as the planet continues to grow and migrate away from its original orbit.  These findings suggest that the planet's non-circular orbit may significantly impact the evolution of its surrounding disk, and may even affect the planet's ability to accrete and grow.  Future observations of young stars in protoplanetary disks can provide valuable insights into the effects of non-planetary orbits, and may shed light on the mechanisms that shape the disk and influence the planet's growth.

The geometric nature of word embeddings in Euclidean space has led to the development of non-parametric models that map words into a shared space. Recent research has suggested moving away from Euclidean space to either hyperbolic space or symmetric positive definite matrices. This paper proposes a novel approach by representing these models as instances of the Hilbert-Schmidt Lie group, allowing for a unified spectral generalization. We show that hyperbolic and Euclidean models can be viewed as subspaces of this general framework. Our findings also indicate that, in practical applications, the symmetric positive definite model performs better than its Euclidean and hyperbolic counterparts.

The initial phase of hydrogen infrastructure development is focused on repurposing
existing natural gas infrastructure to accommodate the increasing use of hydrogen.
This study investigates the feasibility of repurposing existing natural gas
pipelines to transport hydrogen by analyzing the hydrogen demand in New York
State and constructing a pipeline network to meet it. The findings show that
repurposing existing pipelines can efficiently transport approximately 70%
of the state's required hydrogen supply while only using a fraction of the total
required. This approach, known as the "backbone approach," utilizes a limited
number of large pipelines to transport hydrogen, making it a viable option due to
its lower infrastructure replacement costs compared to a dense, smaller pipeline
system.

A recent study on solar cycle 24's sunspot emergence patterns involved analyzing images from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's HMI and AIA instruments, and the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) vector magnetograms. Researchers found a correlation between subsurface and surface magnetic fields, with both showing similar trends and spatial patterns, and the azimuthal alignment of the two fields shared a high coherence level, particularly in specific conditions. Furthermore, the study found that sunspot emergence patterns could serve as indicators of the sun's internal magnetic structure, and the azimuthal alignment of the subsurface and surface fields showed a high coherence, particularly in specific conditions.

In the field of integrated photonics, we've found a way to produce squeezed light within topological phase's built-in protection mechanism. This topological feature ensures the preservation of constant photon number, which, combined with photon loss, leads to an intrinsic squeeze effect. Utilizing a photonic topological insulator made of a silicon waveguide with built-in silicon-vacancy centers, we discovered two mechanical modes with distinct resonance frequencies and observed a unique interaction between them. By pumping one mode at half the resonance frequency, we generated a notable level of squeezed state, which was confirmed by measuring the squeezed state's spectrum and observing the effect through a specific optical pattern. This topological approach allows for the production of a wide range of polarized squeezed light and holds potential for the development of a fully topological integrated quantum information platform.

This study presents a new method for generating drone trajectories in Polysim environment and assesses its performance. The method is then compared with the standard drone model in Polysim using several performance metrics, including time, speed, and acceleration. A unique feature of the research is the implementation of a proposed trajectory planning algorithm, which was evaluated against the standard drone model. The comparison showed that the proposed algorithm produces more efficient time profiles without compromising speed and acceleration. Furthermore, an investigation into the factors influencing drone performance in Polysim using the one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis method revealed that the drone's mass has the greatest impact on its overall performance.

This research focuses on examining the properties of a specific type of linear code called an $F_q$-additive conjugacy code, with the goal of creating a systematic approach to counting these codes when their length is relatively small. By establishing a set of equations, we are able to determine the number of $F_q$-linear $A_C$-conjugacy codes of a specified length. Additionally, in the case where the characteristic of the field, $q$, is equal to two, we derive a formula that describes the structure of the code $A_C$ and uses this formula to determine the number of $F_2$-linear $A_C$-conjugacy codes of a specified length.

The career trajectory of physicists and mathematicians into industry jobs often lacks a defined path, resulting in uncertainty for individuals seeking to transition from academic research to private sectors. To bridge this gap, the 2021 Snowmass Engagement Activity aimed to support physicists and mathematicians in achieving new career goals. This activity offered a series of workshops and discussions focusing on specific employment fields, such as industry, government, and formal education, and provided valuable insights into the skills needed for success in each. Workshops also addressed common challenges faced by HEP researchers transitioning to non-research roles and explored ways to enhance communication among individuals in the various stages of their careers. By promoting interdepartmental dialogue and intergenerational knowledge sharing, the workshops sought to promote cross-disciplinary collaboration. This article aims to summarize key findings from the workshops and provide practical suggestions for supporting the professional development of early and mid-career researchers.

The W boson polarization can be determined from the angle between the top quark's b-quark and the direct W boson product from the lepton.  The influence of the top quark spin is removed by aligning it with the W boson direction.  The W boson polarization can be inferred from the charge of the lepton and the presence of a jet above a certain threshold in the W boson's bosonic decay.  The sensitivity of this method was tested using Monte Carlo simulations of t-bar t and t-bar t-bar t processes at the Large Hadron Collider.  The method showed an ability to measure the W boson polarization in the range of 0.5 to 2.0 with a 1 sigma uncertainty of 0.3 to 0.7.  The method showed an ability to measure the W boson polarization in the range of 0.5 to 2.0 with a 1 sigma uncertainty of 0.3 to 0.7.

We've developed a novel set of sum rules for the ξ-moments of D-meson distribution amplitudes in terms of light-cone distribution amplitudes of local mesons. These new sum rules offer a distinct approach to studying the ξ-moments, in contrast to methods relying on dispersion relations and the AdS/CFT model. The new sum rules enable the determination of ξ-moments of D- and B-mesons, which can be used to analyze D- and B-meson distribution amplitudes and ultimately inform theoretical predictions of D(†) → K- π+ νν̄ and D(†) → K- π+ lepton-lepton decay widths.

This study introduces an eigenvalue theory for power hypergraphs and signed subgraphs, building upon the concept of signed subgraphs as a means to derive the eigenvalues of a power hypergraph from its signed subgraphs. Contrary to existing research, the results of this work demonstrate that the eigenvalues of a power hypergraph are indeed the characteristic values of its signed subgraph counterparts. The theory also provides a framework for analyzing the eigenvalues of power graphs, power hypergraphs, and their combinations, as well as their respective co-eigenvalues. The findings presented here offer a more accurate representation of existing research findings, correcting several misconceptions in prior literature.

This paper examines the application of inter-satellite tracking techniques to satellite navigation in low Earth orbit. A novel approach to localising satellites in orbit utilizes inter-satellite range measurements, which can be integrated with ground-based tracking to enhance precision. Localisation performance was assessed through Monte Carlo simulations for different orbit configurations and measurement types. The results showed that an accuracy of approximately 5-10 meters can be achieved using only inter-satellite range measurements, while combining these with ground-based tracking can improve accuracy to around 1-2 meters.

Our research provides the first-ever measurement of the orbital period decrease of the exoplanet XO-3b, a hot Jupiter orbiting a subgiant star. This planet's unique characteristics make it an ideal candidate for studying the effects of tidal interactions with its host, given its short orbital period and close proximity to its star. Utilizing data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, we discovered a 1.4-s orbital period decrease over 1.8 years in XO-3b, indicating its rapid spin-down due to tidal dissipation. Our analysis revealed that the planet's orbital period is decreasing by 1.0(8) s per year, and we estimated the tidal quality factor of the star to be around $3.3 \times 10^9$. Additionally, we found that the planet's mass is likely to be 0.3-1.6 times Jupiter's mass, and its orbit is expanding at a rate of 0.8(8) mas per year.

We've developed a revolutionary Bayesian calibration method that boosts the accuracy of experiments in astrophysical measurements. By integrating cutting-edge machine learning techniques, our approach enhances the capabilities of established algorithms to a remarkable extent. The method's flexibility enables it to work with various calibration algorithms, and when applied to established techniques, our technique elevates them significantly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to maximum-likelihood exoplanet transit timing measurement and a Gaussian process regression-based white dwarf cooling age calibration methods, further refining them with the addition of periodic and quadratic systematic corrections.

We demonstrate that the genus zero equivariant Gromov-Witten theory of
projective bundles is entirely determined by the theory of the underlying vector
bundle. This leads to a finding that a projective bundle equipped with a
connection over the fundamental group is entirely characterized by its
equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants of genus zero. This result shares parallels
with recent work by Okounkov, Pandharipande, and Papathanasiou, who found that
vector bundles over base $S^1$ are fully identifiable through their
equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants of genus zero.

We establish uniform bounds for the transfer of weights for tensor product L-functions of symmetric square L-functions in the GL_2 context. This achievement enables a comprehensive framework for predicting (non)vanishing of L-functions associated with newforms and, as a consequence, confirms conjectures of Gross and Deligne. Moreover, our findings incorporate automorphic data for tensor products of classical and theta representations and provide an approach to refining the Weyl law for the Neumann matrix of the space of square integrable modular forms.

A recent study on constrained longitudinal data analysis with natural cubic splines has provided a unique perspective on the selection of polynomial coefficients in non-parametric models. By implementing a spline with infinitely adjustable coefficients at each time point, the method enables the assessment of both fixed and random effects in continuous outcomes in clinical trials. The results of the simulation experiments demonstrate the method's efficacy in accurately estimating fixed and random effects, compared to a conventional random effects model. Notably, the method has shown improved accuracy with increasing data points. Furthermore, the analysis of a clinical trial dataset on the safety and efficacy of a drug has confirmed the method's effectiveness in extracting meaningful information from the data.

Our routing protocol, CRAWLING, employs a spatial diffusion model to replicate
bacterial chemotaxis in wireless communication. By utilizing actual node positions,
it accurately captures stochastic behaviors, taking into account the impact of packet
size on routing decisions. CRAWLING's design focuses on balancing the trade-off
between the benefits of increased packet size and the avoidance of dominant
centrality, thereby promoting a more distributed and node-local routing process. 
Numerous simulations have shown CRAWLING's ability to achieve superior packet
delivery reliability while maintaining low hop counts, outperforming protocols like
AODV, ARA, and AOMDV in terms of packet delivery rate, routing latency, and route
variability.

This study examines flat-minima optimization methods in the context of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), particularly on the CIFAR-10 dataset with a ResNet architecture. We investigate two widely-used approaches to achieving scalability through minima optimization, namely stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and weight clipping (WC), and conduct a comparative analysis to assess their performance. Our analysis demonstrates that the two methods exhibit distinct convergence patterns, with a notable difference in final performance. Our results also highlight the importance of careful hyperparameter selection and offer insights into the characteristics of the optimized models.

A parametric FSL device, utilizing a SIS varactor diode, was tested to assess its performance. The device effectively blocks signals above 0.8 MHz while allowing lower frequencies, with the ideal operating conditions being 20V and 150mA. However, the system has a significant insertion loss of 25.2 dB and a power threshold of 0.75W. The device's operation was found to be quite stable, with frequency and voltage fluctuations causing minimal changes in the blocked frequency range. The device's tuning range is also notable, with the addition of voltage levels 1.2v and 1.5v allowing it to cover a wide range of 2.5MHz.

We examine the impact of quarantine measures on an epidemic spreading in a linear network of sources with identical spread patterns, where sources connect to a large number of targets, each of which can be isolated or exposed. We analyze the dynamics of the quarantine protocol, which involves isolating individuals, either those infected or at a random distribution. The quarantine period is a discrete, finite duration $T$. Introducing a quarantine protocol results in the emergence of multiple, isolated epidemics in the long term, with the size of the outbreaks determined by the size of the isolated groups. However, if the number of targets is large enough, these waves can merge under certain conditions. Conversely, if the number of targets is small enough, these conditions are never met. Furthermore, if the number of targets is large enough, these waves can merge under certain conditions. Introducing a quarantine period of length $T$ can either delay the epidemic's peak, accelerate it, or have no effect at all.

We introduce a pioneering approach that integrates both sentence context and structural elements from dependency trees for improved unsupervised term matching. By leveraging context from the sentence that contains the pair of terms to be matched and structural features from the dependency tree linking these terms, our approach yields satisfying results in both domains where it was tested. (1) In the medical domain, combining context and structural elements resulted in precision of 0.83 and recall of 0.74 when matching a set of medical terms. (2) In the domain of chemical names, context and structural elements were used to match a set of chemical names with high precision of 0.85 and recall of 0.75.

We investigate the Poisson Boolean model in d-dimensional space where each component is scaled by ϱ^1/d. For a large ϱ, the probability that a cluster originating at the center survives is at most O(ϱ^-2) for the sum of the maximum cluster sizes, a value that is at most the maximum cluster size itself. This implies that a similar model where components are independent and identically distributed with a distribution μ and ϱ is large, the expected size of a cluster in this model is at most O(integral of x^2 μ(x)dx) with an upper bound that is at most O(integral of μ(x)dx) for the sum of the maximum cluster sizes, a value that is at most constant times the maximum cluster size itself.

This study utilizes three-dimensional simulations to investigate how stellar cores evolve, with a focus on the role of the self-gravity and rotation. We examine the development of equilibrium states under various conditions, including both rotating and non-rotating barotropic and baroclinic environments, to better understand how internal forces and density gradients contribute to stellar structures. We've developed an innovative method for creating initial models from linearized simulations, allowing us to study how three-dimensional effects grow in smaller, more stable star systems.
