We've also created a new approach to analyzing and fitting the results of these simulations, to better understand how internal forces and density gradients shape the structures of stars.

A novel, generalized structure scalars are formulated for the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetime with an inhomogeneous mass distribution and non-zero transverse pressure. These structure scalars' properties are examined in a more complex spacetime than a static, uniform LTB model. We explore the impact of the potential terms on the scalar's minimum value and its connection to the Ricci 4-scattering matrix.

Quantum nonlocality is a phenomenon that can be used to demonstrate the violation of local realism. It is an essential aspect of quantum theory that can be leveraged to develop secure cryptographic protocols. In contrast to classical systems, quantum systems enable the hiding of local data in a multi-partite state. However, achieving this hidden locality requires specific sets of nonlocal systems. In this study, we have identified a fundamental link between nonlocal systems and hidden locality. We have also developed a method to estimate the nonlocality of local sets using quantum correlations. Our research demonstrates that any local hiding scenario can be transformed into a nonlocal hiding scenario with the assistance of a specific quantum source.

The goal of this study is to develop accurate two-class or tri-class predictors for web page visual attention using eye-tracking data, automatically identifying areas of user interest without requiring user input. To this end, we utilize multilabel classification techniques, specifically a multilabel extension of the $k$-NN classifier and a multilabel SVM, to build predictors. These are then compared to supervised and unsupervised clustering algorithms, including hierarchical clustering and the DBSCAN algorithm, in a benchmarking scenario. Evaluation is carried out using the X-ray eye-tracking dataset, a large and challenging multilabel dataset. Our results show that the multilabel $k$-NN and multilabel SVM classifiers outperform the competing methods, with multilabel SVM delivering the best overall performance.

A novel 2-bit transmissive Reflective Intelligence (RI) element is introduced that significantly expands the range of phase modulation capabilities compared to existing 2-bit solutions. The proposed transmissive RIS element features a combination of a variable thickness and wedge-shaped design. The thickness of the RIS element is adjusted to fine-tune the relative phase shift, while the angled facets enable a broader set of outgoing angles to be produced with the same phase shift, effectively increasing the phase coverage. The design's versatility and adaptability make it an ideal choice for applications requiring wide phase modulation ranges. The performance of the 2-bit transmissive RIS element is demonstrated through its application in improving communication systems, particularly in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios and deep-subwavelength structures.

We suggest a novel approach to the traditional reinforcement learning task by converting it into a linear problem in the context of Markov decision processes based on linear models. This reformulation yields benefits for both theoretical and practical purposes. Firstly, it facilitates sample-efficient offline learning under minimal assumptions regarding the quality of the provided data. Additionally, it enables the incorporation of a wide array of regularization techniques commonly employed in machine learning, thus allowing for more effective handling of data with high dimensions. Furthermore, this reformulation provides a more precise understanding of the conditions required for achieving convergence in the context of offline learning. Finally, our results indicate that when combined with an effective online learning algorithm, our linear-problem formulation can lead to the most efficient use of data in the context of Markov decision processes based on linear models, even in the context of online learning.

In this paper, we explore how to apply algebraic K-theory to higher inductive types within the framework of homotopy type type theory.  Our approach has its roots in classical K-theory, which can be seen as representing the K-group of a space by applying a functor that maps each smooth space to its K-group of scalar bundles.  In the context of higher inductive types, this can be achieved through the use of type theory's cellular complex, allowing us to apply the same functors that were used in the classical setting to higher inductive types within the type theory.  Our focus is on the specific case of a higher inductive type space, which can be understood as the type-theoretic equivalent of a space, and can be broken down into its fundamental components.  We demonstrate that the K-theory of a higher inductive type space shares similar properties with the K-theory of a classical space, including the relationship between its homotopy groups and cohomology groups.  Our findings also reveal a close connection between the K-theory of a higher inductive type space and its one-point type, which serves as a fundamental example of a space.

We conducted a detailed study of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) in the center of the galaxy M31, utilizing the MMT spectrograph to collect high-resolution velocity field data on its surrounding stars. Our research involved tracking the star motion over a period of 10 years, providing the most comprehensive velocity map of the central region of M31 to date. Our findings reveal that the galaxy's stars are not in a state of dynamic balance with the SMBH, resulting in a calculated velocity offset of 1 to 4.3 kilometers per second at a distance of one kiloparsec from the SMBH. Our data also show that the galaxy's stars are not rotating around the SMBH in a consistent pattern, but rather exhibit random motions. Our research suggests that the SMBH and the galaxy are not in a state of stable co-rotation, consistent with the idea that the galaxy's stars are being influenced by the SMBH through chaotic scattering. Our findings also imply that the SMBH is not the cause of the observed star motions, but rather that the galaxy's stars are being affected by other galactic forces.

Recent research has revealed that periodic solutions exist in the three-body problem under the condition that two objects are aligned in a line. This paper explores a specific case where a central object is surrounded by two orbiting objects of equal mass, with the central object experiencing external forces. We establish that there are periodic orbits with the central object at a distance equal to the average of the other two, and also find evidence of a periodic arc when the central object is at a maximum distance from the others.

A crucial challenge in fluorescence microscopy is interpreting the light emitted from a group of molecules when the spacing between them is extremely close. To address this issue, researchers have developed a mathematical framework that analyzes how the light from various sources blends together, affecting the detectability of individual sources. Their model, which takes into account the distribution of photoelectrons, has been used to examine the impact of nearby molecules on the detectability of a target and on the accuracy of position estimation in a specific experiment. As a result, it provides a basis for understanding how the density of a molecule affects the accuracy of position detection in optical microscopy.

User preference modeling is a critical issue in e-commerce recommendation systems. Currently, most models focus on understanding user behaviors through recent interactions and global patterns, but they fail to uncover the connections between behaviors and their local implications. To address this issue, we propose a new model called Local Behavior Aware eCommerCe (LBAC) to capture users' overall preferences by combining their global and local patterns of behavior. LBAC uses a behavior-aware transformer to integrate behaviors with their local implications and a novel multi-behavioral attention mechanism to capture users' overall preferences. Our experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that LBAC outperforms existing user preference models.

Graph embedding techniques have been extensively researched in recent years, with a wide array of applications including social network analysis and information retrieval. Notably, the Graph Convolutional Network has been a groundbreaking innovation in graph representation learning. Building upon this concept, we have developed a novel graph embedding approach that leverages geodesic similarity to learn node representations. By employing a deep neural network to calculate geodesic distances, our method can be applied to various graph analysis tasks. Moreover, we have designed a new loss function that efficiently samples and aggregates geodesic distances, leading to more accurate graph representations. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method surpasses multiple baseline models, including GCN, SGC, and UGC, on both node classification and node clustering tasks.

This research investigates how non-orthogonal sequences enhance the performance of uplink grant-free technology in the downlink time slot, specifically focusing on support for the scheduling of multiple users. A performance improvement is achieved by utilizing a factorization approach to identify a set of active users based on the detection of sparse multi-carrier signals in the complex domain. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this method can decrease the average detection error rate by half when compared to the use of orthogonal sequences, while also enabling the scheduling of multiple users with minimal increase in the number of pilot symbols.

We introduce a linear algebraic technique, the Decoder-Expander Based Factorisation (DEBIF) algorithm, for extracting sparse codes from linear measurements via factorisation of a corresponding matrix. DEBIF builds on prior work involving the Decoder-Expander algorithm, now adapted for code lengths that are not constrained to be prime. The algorithm refines the code by iteratively expanding and contracting codes until reaching the target code length. Theoretical analysis under the assumption of ideal coders demonstrates exponential decay in error rate, and numerical simulations with Gaussian coders up to 500 bits confirm this, with performance improving as the number of bits increases.

This study introduces differentiable adversarial data augmentation (DAIA), a technique utilizing spatial transformers to dynamically adjust images in response to models in progress. By leveraging this interaction, DAIA creates a mutually beneficial cycle between the model and the optimizer, leading to enhanced performance. Our experiments demonstrate that DAIA provides significant benefits, particularly on models nearing peak performance, and surpasses current top-tier image classification techniques. DAIA's dynamic approach also facilitates model adaptation to new domains through a single step, and our experiments show that it can successfully generalize to unseen datasets with improved performance.

For an arbitrary connected, locally compact space, the long-term behavior of specific 2-local spatial derivations on infinite-dimensional matrix-valued map algebras is investigated. In the context of the connected, locally compact group $\mathbb R$ and the associated non-commutative $C^*$-dynamical system, the study examines the behavior of 2-local spatial derivations on infinite-dimensional, uniformly bounded self-adjoint matrix-valued processes. It is demonstrated that such derivations converge in the long term, with the limiting process exhibiting independence and stationarity. This process is determined up to unique scalar multiplication by the spectrum of the dynamical system. In addition, the case of the duality pair $(\mathbb R, \mathbb R_*)$ is also analyzed, yielding similar conclusions.

In our research, we delve into the geometric characteristics of the Berry connection within a two-level system that experiences an avoided crossing. We investigate the associated Adiabatic Polarization Surface (APS) and discover that the topological structure of Berry's phase exhibits a striking reversal when moving between the gap and across the gap in parameter space. This leads to the existence of two distinct APS topological invariants, each corresponding to a different regime of motion. We discover that the APS topological invariants can be directly linked to the polarisation surface's topological properties and propose a method to extract the APS topological invariants from a polarisation surface's winding number. We validate our findings by comparing the results to the predictions made by a theoretical model.

We investigate SOC-compactons in spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensates, specifically focusing on the form of Rabi coupling where $\Omega_R=\Omega_R^0+i\Omega_R^\prime$. Our analysis reveals that SOC-compactons occur under more lenient conditions with SO coupling than in its absence and that this form of $\Omega_R$ uniquely enables stable compacton solutions for atoms with spin 1/2. Furthermore, we demonstrate that spin 1 bosons can also support stable compactons when an appropriate form of $\Omega_R$ is introduced. Our results also show that SO coupling and $\Omega_R$ independently lead to an increase in the compacton's speed of sound and a decrease in its speed of sound dispersion.

The deviation in the decay width ratios of certain semileptonic b-quark decays to c-quark from expected values in the heavy quark limit can be used to estimate the mass difference between the b-quark mass and its renormalized counterpart derived from heavy quark charm mass.  This is achieved through the utilization of the experimental data on the lepton energy moments obtained by the Belle and BaBar Collaborations.  This method's accuracy is enhanced by the inclusion of next-to-next-to-next-to leading order corrections to the lepton energy moments.  Through the application of the method, an estimate of the mass difference between the b-quark mass and its renormalized counterpart of approximately 2.5 GeV is determined, which is in line with the results from other methods within the heavy quark effective theory.

We investigate the approximation of function spaces within a smooth manifold M, 
with an action of a Lie group G, where the space of functions is defined on the 
orbit space M/G and has values in another space, typically R or C, and is equipped 
with a specific group homomorphism. This setting naturally encompasses various 
spaces of continuous functions, such as C(K), where K is a compact subset of M, 
under the continuous action of G, with the action being induced by a specific 
Lie group action. Our research focuses on the approximation of the orbit space M/G 
and its dual space under certain conditions, such as the existence of a specific 
group homomorphism, and its implications on the approximation of the original space 
of functions on M.

A future muon collider has the potential to significantly improve our understanding of the electroweak sector, especially in relation to heavy axion-like particles (ALPs) that may not be accessible through proton-based colliders. By serving as a complementary tool, the muon collider can provide new insights by detecting a variety of ALP signatures, including their impact on muon beams, undetected energy signals, and events with inconsistent muon momentum. Advanced machine learning techniques can enhance the accuracy of event classification and reduce the influence of systematics, ultimately leading to enhanced sensitivity in the search for ALPs. By leveraging these techniques, the analysis can be optimized, incorporating multiple variables and improving overall sensitivity.

To accelerate the development of new hardware ideas, we introduce MetaSys, a flexible framework that enables rapid creation and testing of dynamic, meta-programmable systems. By leveraging the QEMU system emulator and its open-source, extensible architecture, MetaSys streamlines the process of designing and implementing both uniprocessor and multiprocessor systems. The framework's modular design, grounded in the RISC-V ISA, allows for the integration of various layers, such as device models, operating systems, and applications. By stacking these layers, MetaSys facilitates the exploration of innovative, cross-layer solutions for hardware and software challenges.

The analysis of biotechnology processes such as CHO-K1 suspension growth in micro-particles is complicated by the scarcity of data and the high cost of experimentation. This makes it difficult to train reliable models, which is why a new approach is proposed to address this challenge. A Twin-VAE, consisting of a latent space with separate dimensions for process conditions and cell characteristics, is developed to enable data transfer between different experiments. This is achieved through a novel transfer function that guides the VAE to learn the shared underlying dynamics across training datasets. This Twin-VAE is then paired with a deep Q-Network to learn optimal control policies for various objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the Twin-VAE in data transfer learning scenarios with simulated and real-world bioprocess data.

We introduce an innovative method to establish the notion of a strong solution as being equivalent to a weak solution for certain types of parabolic and elliptic partial differential equations, without relying on the smoothness of the boundary or the regularity of the coefficients, thus filling a gap in existing mathematical theory. This approach also enables the transformation of any weak solution to a strong one under specific boundary conditions. Our technique has been successfully applied to a homogeneous Dirichlet problem and a non-homogeneous Neumann problem.

In this research, we introduce the Fourier Recurrent Unit, a novel approach to creating a Fourier neural layer, which is capable of efficiently propagating gradients in its output back to the hidden states, similar to how neural oscillations work. By employing this method, we can design recurrent neural networks that exhibit stability without needing to enforce exploding/vanishing gradients. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach through experiments on various datasets, including a simple problem and a more complex task of generating human-like speech. The results confirm that our proposed method achieves stable gradient propagation and superior performance compared to traditional recurrent neural networks.

This paper investigates the pure exploration problem in bandit optimization with feedback from a black box, which is a key component of the active learning framework. The generative and online variants of this problem differ significantly, with the former allowing for simultaneous query and feedback collection, while the latter present a sequential challenge where queries are made after receiving an oracle response. Our focus is on the online version of this problem, which is commonly referred to as the active linear bandits problem. In this context, we propose an algorithm called S-ALB that leverages a combination of the standard Thompson sampling technique and a self-normalized approach to optimize the query process. Our analysis shows that S-ALB is a consistent estimator with a finite-sample regret bound that scales sublinearly with time and is also asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to a more complex setting in which the data follows a Markovian process, and we demonstrate that S-ALB can effectively handle this scenario by deriving a regret bound that scales linearly with time and is also asymptotically optimal.

Our research reveals that the spin of attosecond electrons produced in a laser-driven plasma wake is influenced by the presence of a strong external magnetic field. These spin-polarized electrons are generated through a specific Compton scattering process involving the laser and plasma electrons. The spin direction of these electrons is determined by the alignment of the laser field and the plasma wake. The study found that the spin of the produced electrons exhibits a distinct behavior in response to the magnetic field, with a non-magnetic component decreasing at 4.8 Tesla and a remaining magnetic component displaying a distinct magnetic field dependence. The study further found that the production of these spin-polarized electrons can be enhanced by adjusting the plasma density and laser intensity.

This paper explores the underlying causes of mutations, which are sudden and unanticipated genetic alterations.  We examine the role of vital fields generated by energetic sources in biological systems and their impact on DNA.  We investigate the mutation process as a result of these fields interacting with DNA, specifically considering the mutation effects on the DNA's entropy and structure.  Our analysis reveals that this mutation process does not randomly alter the DNA's genetic code, but instead results in a more resilient and adaptable genetic entity.  We also discover that mutations driven by these vital fields differ from those caused by random genetic alterations in their characteristics and implications for biological systems.  This work also delves into the relationship between the mutation rate and the distance between energetic sources in the context of vital field-driven mutations.  We examine the mutation process as a result of these fields interacting with DNA, providing insights into the mechanisms behind mutations and their significance in biological systems.

The growing availability of open data has created new possibilities for analyzing Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) ecosystems worldwide. However, the current lack of standardization and interoperability among data sources hampers a comprehensive understanding of these ecosystems and makes it difficult to make comparisons and conduct cross-country analyses. To address this, we propose a common data model that enables the integration of various data sources, standardizes the content and structure of the data, and facilitates interoperability. This, in turn, allows for a unified and interconnected global STI data ecosystem, providing a deeper understanding of research system dynamics and enabling more effective policy decisions.

Low-level programming elements known as Native Development Kit (NDK) are used in Android applications to access device hardware. Although these elements are crucial, they pose a risk to user privacy through side-channel leaks that occur when executing device hardware operations. We developed an approach to identify these side-channel leaks by analyzing the NDK functions' code. Our system initially gathers the list of NDK functions that could potentially introduce side-channel leaks. Next, it generates the functions that could lead to leaks by combining the gathered list with the functions involved in the device hardware operations. The potential leaked information is then determined by analyzing the side-channel signals associated with the leaked functions. We developed an approach to identify these side-channel signals by analyzing the side-channel signals associated with the device hardware operations. Using this approach, we examined 1,000 randomly selected NDK functions from Android NDK r23 and discovered 16 functions that could potentially introduce side-channel leaks. We developed a proof-of-concept tool named NativeSideLeaks and implemented it as an extension of the popular security tool, Sanitizer. We tested NativeSideLeaks on 20 Android applications and discovered 16 potential side-channel leaks.

The massive-scale and decentralized nature of the Ethereum blockchain has driven the rapid growth of the price of cryptocurrency, with high-cost transactions exceeding $100,000 in recent times. This has led to increased interest in identifying key players within Ethereum ego networks. However, current analyses primarily focus on static analysis methods, which are insufficient for capturing the dynamic relationships between influential individuals. This study proposes a novel approach to uncovering key players within these networks through a temporal analysis method. We examine the temporal characteristics of ego networks on Ethereum, including node centrality and community structures, and demonstrate that our approach can effectively identify and distinguish the most influential participants in different transaction types.

The LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ (LAO/STO) interface, a remarkable oxide interface with an ultra-thin electronic channel, has been found to exhibit extraordinary properties such as superconductivity, metal-insulator transition, and magnetism. The origin of these properties is linked to the high-mobility charge carriers within this channel. The existence of these carriers can be influenced by illumination, a phenomenon that has been studied in detail using the LAO/STO interface as a model system. This review explores the current understanding of the high-mobility carriers within LAO/STO and discusses how they can be controlled through light. The high-mobility carriers within LAO/STO possess unique characteristics including rapid changes in concentration, mobility, and Hall coefficient in response to short laser pulses, as well as photoinduced changes in magnetism and superconductivity. The high-mobility carriers within LAO/STO offer a unique platform for studying light-induced phase transitions and the interaction between light and matter at the interface of condensed matter physics.

We introduce an ordering of pomset proofs that preserves the logical implications of pomset logic and demonstrate that it's a polynomial delay equivalent to BV's. This enables us to establish a definition for provability in pomset logic that is compatible with the $\mathcal{NML}$ framework, where we also examine the complexity of associated problems, revealing a new complexity hierarchy within pomset logic that is distinct from the hierarchy in first-order logic.

Using Macdonald polynomials, we re-examine the five-term relation found by Garsia and Mellit for the symmetric group, and we generalize it to the Coxeter Weyl group of type D, developing a combinatorial proof for this generalization. Our approach relies on constructing detailed, basis-like combinatorial structures within the group algebra, which in turn enable us to derive a characteristic polynomial, and we demonstrate that this method can be effectively applied to any Weyl group.

Astronomical surveys need to know how far away galaxies are, which can be done using spectroscopic redshifts. Our new method, called RedshiftNet, uses artificial neural networks to identify and understand the patterns in galaxy spectra. By training RedshiftNet to recognize the different parts of a galaxy's spectrum, we can locate the absorption lines caused by galaxies moving through interstellar medium. Our model can accurately find these lines and calculate the galaxies' redshifts, even when the absorption is weak. Our results show that RedshiftNet can identify the galaxies' redshifts with a high degree of accuracy, an average root mean square error of 0.0008, and can process a large number of spectra in a short amount of time. Our method has the potential to be used on a wide range of galaxy surveys, both in space and on Earth, which can be done using space-based telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and Earth-based telescopes like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

This paper describes a Bayesian decision support system, which is a tool for evaluating how policy changes impact costs associated with operational delays in public transportation. The tool uses probabilistic reasoning to provide uncertainty quantification of results from policy simulations. An implementation of this system is demonstrated within the MATSim simulation platform. The flexibility of this MATSim policy simulator allows for easy integration of the Bayesian decision support system into a complex policy evaluation pipeline.

This study examines the zero-field, ground-state properties of a two-electron system in a pseudo-spin Hamiltonian system with strong spin-orbit interactions. The focus is on the effects of finite system sizes on the ground-state energy and expectation values when using the infinite system's exact wave function as a basis. The analysis considers both a singlet state with all electrons in the valence shell and a triplet state with one unpaired electron in the outer shell. The results are compared to those obtained from the QC-DMRG method, which exactly recovers the FCI energy for the singlet state but not for the triplet state. The investigation also explores the ground-state properties predicted by the unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) method and the effects of finite system sizes on the ground-state energy and expectation values.

We investigate a scenario where a dark matter particle is a singlet majoron originating from the type-I seesaw model, which aligns with recent muon magnetic moment and dark matter relic abundance observations, specifically in the 200-600 GeV mass range. This singlet interacts with leptons via a dimension-5 effective coupling, which also enables it to interact with standard model leptons via a dimension-9 coupling. As a result, the singlet can induce lepton flavor violating decays, such as muon-to-electron transitions, which can be probed by the Mu3e experiment. We examine the experimental constraints on this dark matter scenario and the resulting implications on the Mu3e experiment's sensitivity.

A groundbreaking approach called the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) has successfully predicted complex time-dependent patterns in various natural phenomena. Building upon this innovation, we have adapted FNO for simulating time-dependent tidal flows in coastal areas. By applying FNO to a dataset of high-resolution numerical model simulations, we have achieved a remarkable speedup in computing tidal flows compared to traditional numerical methods. In particular, our FNO-based approach can accelerate simulations by up to 4000 times for point-wise evaluations and 500 times for mesh-based evaluations, all while maintaining high accuracy. This breakthrough has significant implications for large-scale coastal flooding models that rely on extensive numerical simulations.

A joint analysis platform called Cosmo, designed to facilitate collaborative research in cosmic microwave background studies, has been developed using the Python language and NIFTy for data analysis. This software is highly adaptable and can be used to analyze various types of data models. To further enhance the platform's capabilities, Cosmo features a modular structure that allows for the integration of multiple data models. Furthermore, Cosmo features a data-driven approach to processing, including the ability to perform joint likelihood calculations and Bayesian inference. To further the understanding of dark energy and cosmology, researchers have utilized Cosmo to perform a series of experiments using both mock data and real-world observational data from the Planck and ACT datasets. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Cosmo in analyzing complex datasets and its potential to be a valuable resource for the cosmology community. To ensure the platform's continued success, community involvement is essential for its further development.

Turing's reaction-diffusion model has been found to produce a wide variety of patterns across both biological and non-biological systems. However, its applicability in complex networks with many interconnected components has not been extensively explored. Previous studies have demonstrated the emergence of Turing patterns in regular lattice networks, but the results were largely dependent on the specific model used. Our research, on the other hand, examines the Turing instability in complex networks with a non-uniform structure, and we find that diffusion rates between activator and inhibitor species have a unique optimal point that maximizes instability. Furthermore, we show that the Turing patterns observed in these networks are sensitive to noise and have different stability characteristics compared to those in regular lattices.

We investigate the impact of a hidden symmetry on a $\varphi^4$ theory with a phantom field, $Z$, which is coupled to the scalar in a specific way. When the phantom field is absent, the theory's classical symmetry gives rise to a conserved current, but the addition of the phantom field restores the symmetry, but at the cost of one dimension. Interestingly, the resulting symmetry, even in its reduced form, still yields a conserved current, which can be confirmed through a direct computation. This computation involves evaluating the divergence of the supercurrent in a specific gauge, where the phantom field's potential drops off, confirming the result. This recovery of the conserved current is achieved by a renormalization process that involves a specific counterterm, which is part of a finite set of relevant operators.

Our comprehensive study examines the electronic properties of GaAs nanowires with varying core diameters, from 5nm to 100nm, using transport measurements and ab-initio calculations. The results show that the energy at the quantized plateau exhibits a linear relationship with the nanowire's radius. The energy difference between the energy levels at the 2nd and 3rd quantized plateaus is used to determine the effective mass of the conduction band, which is found to be close to the mass of conduction electrons in bulk GaAs. The data also indicate that the energy gap between the energy levels at the 2nd and 3rd quantized plateaus decreases as the core diameter increases, signifying a decrease in energy confinement. The results from the energy gap measurements are consistent with the energy level calculations, showing that the energy confinement weakens as the core diameter increases. The study's findings can be applied to the design of quantum devices such as quantum point contacts and quantum devices based on nanowires.

We introduce an approach to fine-tune pre-trained dialogue models, enabling them
to infer an opponent's preferences from limited conversation data and perform
strategically, without explicit training on this task. Our method, based on
sequence models, utilizes a classification layer to identify preference-related
utterances as positive or negative signals, which are incorporated into the
dialogue response generation process. We demonstrate that this method effectively
detects preferences and generates coherent, strategically playable dialogue
across multiple game settings, including Diplomacy and The Cartoon Wars.

The behavior of different types of strings coexisting in the same spatial area is examined under specific worldsheet and bulk constraints. A requirement of invariance under conformal quantum conditions restricts the tension scalar's behavior for particular domain walls with intrinsic stress. The energy-momentum tensor for these walls is examined within the context of the Brans-Davis-Maxwell framework. A constraint is placed on the string's central charge by the condition of compatibility with the dilaton's equation of motion. A specific bound is established for string central charge in the presence of a domain wall.

In experimental psychology, researchers often create extensive databases containing various treatments and numerous items to be tested. This process is challenging due to the need to block item pairs with conflicting requirements, a concern that becomes more complex when treatments and items are continuously added. To tackle this challenge, known as the Online Blocking Problem, researchers have devised a method that utilizes pigeonhole design, allowing for the dynamic assignment of treatments without prior knowledge of item requirements. This approach is compared to a traditional method, demonstrating its superiority in multiple scenarios. When treatments and items are added sequentially, our method offers improved performance, specifically reducing the average block size by 10.6% and 6.5% compared to a random assignment and an optimized method, respectively.

The electronic properties of the interface between gamma-Al2O3 and silicon were studied using high-resolution scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Our research found that the original, unmodified interface exhibits unique energy bands, distinct from the typical metal-insulator properties. However, introducing certain elements into the interface altered its energy bands, causing them to resemble those of a metal-insulator system. Our data also show that the energy bands at the interface exhibit distinct characteristics at various energy levels, such as a peak at approximately 0.7 eV and a dip at around 0.4 eV. By analyzing these features, we were able to understand the complex interactions happening at the interface and identify the roles of various energy states.

We explore the characteristics of self-similar gravitational collapse in a system incorporating Einstein-axion-dilaton components. Our research reveals that these collapse solutions give rise to spacetime dilation and internal transformations equivalent to the collapse of a scalar-charge across a gravitational event horizon. Furthermore, we find that the collapse solutions separate the spacetime into distinct regions: a past causal area, where the collapse solution applies, and an outside spacelike asymptotic region, where the solution approaches a stationary state. In the interior spacetime, the solution evolves into a naked singularity surrounded by an atypical Cauchy horizon. Interestingly, we observe that the spacetime dilation and internal transformations across this Cauchy horizon are distinct from one another, suggesting that the singularity is accessible in a non-intuitive manner. Our findings are significant, as they imply that the well-known singularity theorems may not be applicable in this system, leading to the potential for the naked singularity to be stable.

This research investigates the impact of dismantling shipping cartels through mergers and acquisitions on the shipping industry, utilizing data from the United States over a period of 20 years at a monthly frequency. By combining data on ship size and weight, I develop a dynamic spatial price and quantity model that accounts for unobserved market conditions and factors influencing shipping rates. The results indicate that the dissolution of shipping cartels led to increased average shipping rates and a decrease in total shipping volume, specifically showing that the acquisition of flagships by dominant carriers had a significant positive effect on rates. Additionally, I find that the increased competition from the acquisition of flagships was the primary driver behind the increase in shipping rates, and that the acquisition of secondary ports had a much less significant effect.

The field of anomaly detection encompasses a diverse range of techniques, which have been categorized into various approaches.  Despite the abundance of available algorithms, selecting the most suitable one for a specific dataset is still a challenging task, particularly in real-world scenarios where data often lacks labeling.  To address this issue, researchers have developed a comprehensive evaluation framework that utilizes simulated data to compare the performance of offline and online anomaly detection algorithms.  The framework's results reveal that, while more efficient online algorithms are often less effective than their offline counterparts, they are still outperformed by algorithms that require the recalculation of models, which can lead to time-consuming computations.  To mitigate this limitation, researchers have introduced a new online algorithm that maintains a compact model and achieves comparable results to its offline counterpart.  The framework's findings also highlight the importance of considering the performance of anomaly detection algorithms across various data distributions, which is crucial for evaluating their robustness.  To this end, researchers have developed a new evaluation metric that assesses an algorithm's ability to adapt to unseen data.  The framework's results demonstrate that online algorithms can be improved by incorporating this metric and suggests that algorithms that are designed to adapt to changing data distributions may be more effective in real-world scenarios.

A novel approach to segment gliomas using deep learning is presented, focusing on enhancing the accuracy of manual segmentation by radiologists. This method utilizes a combination of Convolutional Neural Networks and a 3D U-Net model to leverage the rich information within MRI scans. By integrating 3D data analysis, the proposed method enables the separation of tumor types while allowing for the adjustment of segmentation results in line with manual predictions. In clinical trials, the proposed method demonstrated superior performance in comparison to current standards, exhibiting high reliability in repeated applications.

The spin transport mechanism in insulators has been a subject of extensive research, particularly with the discovery of the spin Seebeck effect (SSE). Researchers have been studying the behavior of triplons in the insulating magnet Cs2Cu2Mo2O2, which exhibits a unique magnetic structure, to gain insights into the SSE. An investigation of the triplon spin SSE in this material was conducted, and the results showed that the triplon spin diffusion is distinct from that of spin waves in other magnets. Furthermore, the triplon thermal diffusion was found to be unique compared to other types of phonons and spin waves. An analysis of the triplon spin Seebeck coefficient revealed a significant temperature dependence, which can be attributed to the competition between triplon-hopping and triplon-phonon interactions.

This paper introduces the concept of nets within the framework of topological groups, building upon their analogues in metric spaces. The authors establish a connection between the statistical convergence of nets within nets spaces and the topological groups' context, generalizing classical findings to various nets spaces such as sequences, biorthogonal nets and so on across different group structures. Additionally, the study examines the intersection of two distinct forms of convergence - statistical and topological convergence - along with highlighting applications to the Fourier and theorems of Hausdorff Young.

This study explores the application of discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods to Rosenau equation, which is a non-linear hyperbolic equation, using a variational approach. A thorough investigation into the issue of thread-unsafe element-wise updates is conducted, and two strategies are proposed to mitigate this problem. The proposed methods involve formulating a non-conservative numerical scheme, which is conservative in relation to fluxes, and ensuring thread safety through synchronization. Our study also examines the asymptotic accuracy of the proposed method using phase space averaging techniques, which is verified through numerical experiments.

A new, high-performance method for detecting the boundaries of compressible and incompressible fluids in their respective zones within a computational field is proposed. This approach relies on the finite element method for spatial discretization and a custom-made time-dependent boundary detection algorithm. A novel, time-efficient technique is presented that effectively identifies the boundaries of the fluid domain within a computational field. This new method is compared to the widely used level set method and found to offer improved computational efficiency. A detailed description of the algorithm's implementation and its application to various test cases, including a realistic industrial scenario, is provided.

We examine the equilibrium state of many-particle systems composed of
charged interlayer excitons, taking into account Coulomb interactions and a
uniform external potential. The model is based on a tight-binding description
of within-layer excitons and a two-dimensional Coulomb description of
interlayer excitons. A mean-field approximation is used to calculate the
equilibrium density matrix, from which the energy levels and wave functions
are derived. Our calculations show that, in systems with large separation
between layers, the energy associated with the potential interactions is much
larger than that associated with the kinetic energy, resulting in a system that
behaves similarly to a localised electron gas. This system exhibits a
damped
mode of oscillation, characterized by the exchange of energy between the
internal exciton system and the lattice. The frequency of this mode is
inversely proportional to the distance between the layers.

We investigated how accurately the calibration of reference stars can be used to determine the precise radial velocities of other stars in a given dataset, specifically in the context of the SDSS-IV/APOGEE-2 North survey. We used data from the APOGEE-2 North survey, which includes measurements of stars in the Sun's solar system, to analyze the impact of systematic errors in the APOGEE-2 North spectrograph on our understanding of the solar system. We found that the APOGEE-2 North spectrograph has a significant systematic error in the calculation of radial velocities, which is caused by variations in the temperature of the spectrograph's plates. This error is not uniform across the dataset and is not solely the result of random noise. We used a Bayesian model to analyze the impact of the systematic error on the radial velocities of other stars in the survey, which resulted in an average error of about 0.2 kilometers per second. This is a significant improvement over previous estimates of the error, which were about 1.5 kilometers per second. We also found that the APOGEE-2 North spectrograph has a significant systematic error in the calculation of stellar parameters, which is caused by variations in the temperature of the spectrograph's plates. This error is not uniform across the dataset and is not solely the result of random noise. This research highlights the importance of careful calibration and analysis of stellar parameters in the calculation of radial velocities.

We introduce a novel neural architecture designed to handle high-dimensional input data, where the weight parameters scale sub-linearly with input dimensions. Leveraging a recent breakthrough in topological data analysis, our model learns the structure of the input data using a neural computation inspired by the work of Ronan Arbel and co-authors. By mapping the input data into a neural network with specific weight constraints, our architecture achieves state-of-the-art results on a range of benchmark datasets, including the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, a simulated two-dimensional dataset, and a real-world dataset of three-dimensional galaxy distributions. Furthermore, our architecture allows for the efficient generation of new data points, enabling the analysis of complex systems with known input parameters.

A model based on Gamma processes is employed to analyze degradation patterns over time in reliability studies. We develop a Bayesian point estimation approach for modeling unknown Gamma process intensities using Monte Carlo expectation maximization. A simulated study validates the method's effectiveness. Subsequently, the proposed approach is applied to a real-world dataset for two-unit systems with series and parallel configurations.

We utilize the quark coalescence model to analyze the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow, observed in 200 GeV $p$+Au collision data from the RHIC experiment. We compare these findings to theoretical predictions and find that they align with results from other hadrons. Furthermore, our research investigates the relationship between $v_3$ and the longitudinal momentum of particles. We also explore the connection between $v_3$ and the internal properties of particles, specifically their mass, and find that this relationship holds true. Notably, the distribution of $v_3$ in terms of particle mass mirrors that of $v_2$. Additionally, the transverse momentum dependence of $v_3$ for different quark flavors aligns with results from model calculations, suggesting that quark recombination is the dominant factor behind the observed $v_3$ at low momenta.

A region known as the High Speed Stream (HSS) is characterized by high-speed solar wind flowing along the Parker spiral in a relatively smooth manner. However, when it encounters an Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejection (ICME), it exhibits complex and changing behavior, including the formation of a forward shock, a contact surface, and a region of disturbed plasma. By analyzing data from the Solar Orbiter's first encounter with the Sun, we have studied the interaction between the HSS and an ICME observed on November 11, 2020. Due to the unique geometry of this encounter, we have identified a 'wedge-shaped' interface between the HSS and the ICME, and have used this information to develop a 3D model of the interaction. Our model suggests that the contact surface is a combination of a 2D surface and a 3D structure, and we have shown that the surface is located at a specific distance from the Sun. Our findings provide insights into the properties of the ICME and the HSS, and highlight the importance of considering the 3D geometry of the interaction between HSS and ICME.

A new approach to simulating Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks is proposed, grounded in a novel model of node mobility that can generate more realistic long-term patterns and has a proven mathematical basis. This is achieved by employing a Random Waypoint Mobility Model where each node's velocity is randomly distributed, thereby enabling the derivation of analytical expressions for key metrics such as node meeting times and network connectivity. By utilizing this model, simulations of large-scale and low-bandwidth networks can be made statistically reliable. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness by comparing it with a widely used simulation model, showing that it produces more stable and predictable outcomes, especially in scenarios with low connectivity.

The K+ spectrum in exclusive $\Lambda_b^0$ decays into charmonia was studied using an amplitude-based approach that considered Coulomb and strong interactions between charged mesons. Strong interactions, mediated by $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ resonances, were found to have a significant impact on the production of K+K- pairs, resulting in a broad peak in the K+K- invariant mass distribution. This effect was particularly evident in the decay of J/psi, but was significantly reduced in the decays of higher charmonium states, charmonium state with the phi particle. This discovery may provide new insights into the production of these resonances in B-meson decays.

The average slope of a constant method (ASCC) is presented to estimate nuclear masses, enabling the derivation of galilean-invariant second and third order cranking formulae from its basis. By differentiating the ASCC mass with respect to rotation, the second order cranking formulae are derived, which are then compared with conventional cranking formulae. These conventional cranking formulae lack Galilean invariance, a fact demonstrated by their application to the $f_{7/2}$ and $g_{9/2}$ shells. In contrast, the ASCC method yields a galilean-invariant estimate of these mass differences. Furthermore, the ASCC method is extended to third order by considering the average of the second derivative of the ASCC mass with respect to rotation, and the third order cranking formulae are derived. It is shown that the conventional third order cranking formulae lack Galilean invariance, while the ASCC method yields a galilean-invariant estimate of the third order mass effect.

We introduce a novel framework called Abstract Reasoning with Graph Abstractions (ARGA), designed for extracting programs from text-based reasoning tasks by employing graph-based program synthesis techniques. Building upon the concept of abstract machines, ARGA models the reasoning process as a series of graph transformations, which are applied to input graphs to produce output graphs. Our framework is adaptable to various Abstract Reasoning tasks and can be optimized for maximum efficiency by identifying the most critical graph transformations, which are then applied to derive the output program. We showcase the effectiveness of ARGA through its application to two prominent Abstract Reasoning benchmarks, CLARREPL and DeepGraph, by introducing ARGen, a research AR model that outperforms existing approaches on these datasets, while also providing insights into ARGen's strengths and limitations.

This research examines the long-term behavior of solutions to partial differential equations with non-traditional diffusion patterns. The equations in question have a discontinuous and possibly changing direction of flow, and this variation in flow direction can occur in areas where it changes in a way that is not continuous. In the past, researchers have used a particular mathematical approach called the BMO metric to study such systems, but here the authors focus on systems with fluxes that are not necessarily Lipschitz. The fractional maximal function is used to measure the long-term effects of these non-standard diffusion patterns, and the authors demonstrate that the associated exponents can be as high as 2 for systems with certain types of flux variations.

Researchers at the Belle detector have used a dataset of 772 million Belle events to study the decays of B-mesons into specific final states. They have made new measurements of branching fractions for several rare decays involving D-mesons, with results as follows: the branching fraction for a certain type of decay involving a strange and a pion is about 27 times lower than another type of decay involving a D and a pion, while a different type of decay involving a strange and a kaon is actually more likely than a type involving a non-strange and a pion, with a branching fraction about 7 times lower than yet another type of decay involving a non-strange and a pion, with results in line with expectations from the standard model and with alternative methods.

A new technique, the MDD-CF scheme, has been developed to enable full-duplex communication in massive MIMO systems, which involves creating a virtual mirror channel through mirror-reflecting analog beamforming. This method has been found to offer superior performance in high-mobility scenarios compared to in-band and time-division full-duplex schemes. This study investigates the performance of the MDD-CF scheme in high-speed vehicles, taking into account the effects of channel estimation and feedback, as well as channel aging. Theoretical models are developed to quantify the achievable rate of the MDD-CF scheme in high-mobility scenarios, with the results showing that the scheme outperforms in-band and time-division full-duplex schemes by 23% and 7%, respectively. The study also demonstrates that the MDD-CF scheme can maintain its performance even when the age of channel information is as old as 0.5 times the vehicle's delay spread.

Numerous cutting-edge numerical methods have been developed to assess the robustness of differential privacy models. In this study, we focus on a specific challenge: creating efficient algorithms to evaluate privacy assurances within the context of Markov decision processes. Our approach involves adapting the classical backward value iteration algorithm and the least-squares temporal difference algorithm, both of which are essential tools in reinforcement learning. By incorporating numerical evaluations of privacy guarantees, these modified algorithms can provide precise estimates of the maximum possible violations of differential privacy. Our findings demonstrate that the new algorithms offer improved efficiency, scalability, and accuracy compared to existing methods.

Over-the-air (OTA) simultaneous transmission systems require efficient methods to manage interference in wireless communication. A novel approach, referred to as OTS-M, utilizes Walsh-Hadamard transform (WHT) to eliminate inter-user interference in OTA transmission. This technique achieves this by generating unique, orthogonal Walsh-Hadamard codes for each user. As a result, WHT enables the integration of multiple signals at the receiver without interference. This paper introduces OTS-M, a system that leverages WHT. It demonstrates that the conjugate WHT can be used for both modulation and demodulation of symbols, simplifying the transmission process. A mathematical derivation of the system's performance using maximum likelihood demodulation is presented, showing that the system can achieve a bit error rate of $2^{-(d/2)R}$. Furthermore, the required power for OTS-M is analyzed, and it is demonstrated that the system can achieve a power exponent of $\frac{d}{2}+\frac{1}{2}$. This performance is shown to be comparable to the ideal case of isotropic cellular networks. A numerical simulation of OTS-M is presented, which confirms the theoretical findings of the approach.

Let $\sigma$ be a contraction on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and $S$ denote the unit circle in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. This paper aims to establish a correlation between the operator norm and the weighted norm of the action $\sigma$ on the algebra of weighted discrete semigroup functions, denoted as $\ell^1(S,\mathbb{C})$. Specifically, it proves that the weighted norm is less than or equal to the operator norm multiplied by a specific constant $\frac{2\pi}{\sin \delta}$, with $\delta$ being the weighted gap in $S$. Furthermore, it shows that the equality between these norms is attainable when $\sigma$ is a unitary operator on $\mathcal{H}$.

A numerical model of laser melting has been developed to simulate the oscillatory behavior of melt pools on a solid substrate. The model considers the effects of surface tension and thermal Marangoni forces on the melt pool surface, taking into account changes in thermo-physical properties that occur when processing materials with high heating and cooling rates. The model's accuracy was validated through experimental investigations of laser-induced Marangoni flows on Cu, Ag, and Au substrates. The model successfully predicted surface deformation and flow patterns in the melt pools of all materials, as well as the direction of thermal Marangoni vortices, in close agreement with the results of the experiments. The model's findings were further supported by a parametric study that examined the effects of laser power, substrate temperature, and material properties on the size and direction of thermal Marangoni vortices, as well as the resulting surface deformation and flow patterns.

This research focuses on developing a wireless system that enables a Smart IoT Device (SID) to connect to a macro base station or a cloud server using a Vehicle-Borne Intelligent Reflecting Surface (VIRS). The study examines the practical implementation of VIRS in a vehicle-based system, considering real-world limitations. We introduce an innovative control strategy to optimize the number of active IRS elements, taking into account the limited available space on the SID. The results show that the proposed system can achieve substantial improvement in terms of energy efficiency when compared to a conventional system without the integration of VIRS.

We have established a lower bound for the approximate degree of constant-depth circuits, determined by the approximate log-depth majority function complexity threshold. Our result shows that, for a specific set of formulas, their approximate degree is bound by the minimum of a polynomial function and a logarithmic function of input size n. This set of formulas includes majority formulas, and our result implies a lower bound for a polynomial threshold formula with a specific level of depth. Our proof involves a combination of techniques, including a method to transform a polynomial threshold formula into a majority formula with a slightly increased depth, and a method to convert a majority formula into a set of formulas with a specific approximate degree. This latter method uses a local sensitivity theorem, and a hypothesis about a certain complexity of a circuit. If proven, this hypothesis would strengthen our result and establish a higher complexity threshold for a specific circuit.

In this paper, we examine dynamical systems that exhibit an attractor supported on a manifold, with nearby trajectories approaching or cross the separatrix at specific points, and explore the potential for a set of initial conditions that allow for such intersections to occur.

The self-energy matrix of quarks in a strong magnetic field is represented by a Hermitian matrix in the coordinate space, with the real parts of its diagonal elements increased by the constituent quark masses, and the imaginary parts connected with the vector potential via the vector potential's gradient. This results in the appearance of bound states in the quark system, and the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter reveals an increase in the melting point compared to the unperturbed case, and the appearance of a phase transition at a specific magnetic field strength.

The intersection of deep learning and audio-visual correlation learning has led to significant advancements in this area, resulting in numerous deep learning techniques being applied to extract meaningful audio-visual features. These features are then used for various applications, such as action recognition, lip-reading, and speech enhancement. However, the current focus on deep learning has overlooked the benefits of traditional signal processing methods. To address this, a novel deep learning technique is proposed, combining the strengths of both deep and traditional learning approaches. This is achieved through a two-part learning process, where traditional learning modules are used to identify the most effective audio-visual features, and deep learning modules are employed to learn the relationships between these features. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, a new dataset, called the Speech and Lip-Motion Corpus, has been created, containing audio and lip-motion data for applications such as speech enhancement and speech-reading. The proposed method has achieved state-of-the-art performance on this corpus, outperforming other deep learning approaches.

The Linear Ordering Problem involves the assignment of objects to the first available position within a sequence, and its computational complexity is assessed via various parameters. A previous study introduced a multi-level approach to the LOP, utilizing a graph representation and searching for an optimal sequence. However, this strategy's performance is influenced by the chosen graph, and more efficient methods are needed. This research proposes an alternative approach, involving a ranking system inspired by Slater's spectrum, to reduce the LOP's complexity and improve the algorithm's efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that this new strategy significantly outperforms the previous method, allowing for the exact solution of large-scale LOP instances within a reasonable time frame and surpassing the state-of-the-art results obtained by the multi-level approach.

We investigate the occurrence of quantum and thermal phase slips in a specific type of superconducting loop that incorporates a Josephson junction and an inductive element, both subjected to thermal fluctuations near its critical temperature.  By using a method that accounts for the interplay between thermal and quantum fluctuations in a loop that is subject to thermal fluctuations, we are able to derive a general expression for the probability of quantum and thermal phase slips.  This expression is then used to calculate the rate of thermal and quantum tunneling in a loop that is subject to thermal fluctuations.  Our findings show that thermal tunneling rates are significantly higher than previously predicted by existing theories, and that thermal tunneling is more probable than quantum tunneling.  Additionally, we found that thermal tunneling rates are significantly higher than quantum tunneling rates, and that thermal tunneling rates are proportional to the critical temperature of the loop.  Our findings also show that thermal tunneling rates are significantly higher than previously predicted by existing theories, and that thermal tunneling rates are significantly higher than quantum tunneling rates in a loop that is subject to thermal fluctuations.  This is a significant result, and it highlights the importance of understanding the interplay between thermal and quantum fluctuations in a loop that is subject to thermal fluctuations.  This interplay is a key factor that affects the thermal and quantum tunneling rates in a loop that is subject to thermal fluctuations.

Temporal regular path queries (TRPQs) are a powerful tool for querying graph databases that track changes over time. Unlike previous languages that limited queries to specific vertices and edges, TRPQs allow for more complex pattern matching on temporal graphs. This more flexible approach is achieved by matching patterns against vertices, edges, or arbitrary node sequences. Furthermore, to accommodate various graph storage formats, TRPQs can utilize edge-labels to define edge meanings. This enables the use of the same pattern language regardless of the graph's structure. To evaluate the performance of TRPQs, we developed a new formalism and a more efficient algorithm that outperforms existing solutions by up to three orders of magnitude in most cases.

The properties and behaviors of free radicals, such as CH3, are crucial in understanding many chemical reactions, but their characteristics have been difficult to study at extremely cold temperatures, such as ultracold and degenerate conditions.  By using a unique method involving a laser cooling technique, which involves a multi-step process, researchers successfully captured and cooled a large number of molecules, specifically 10^4, to an ultracold state, resulting in a significant breakthrough in the study of the CH3 radical.  By employing a specific method to measure the interactions between these ultracold radicals, researchers were able to determine the properties of the free radical, revealing that it behaves as a polar molecule, with a significant implication for the study of ultracold molecular condensates.

The Swift-XRT has been a key tool in identifying and tracking a vast array of transient and persistent X-ray sources. However, its limited field of view and exposure time hinder the simultaneous monitoring of numerous sources. To address this challenge, a Living Swift-XRT Point Source catalogue was established to enable real-time source monitoring. This is achieved by cross-referencing Swift-XRT data against existing catalogues, identifying sources that require follow-up observations. To further enhance its capabilities, the catalogue now incorporates data from the XMM-Newton and ROSAT mission's all-sky surveys. This expansion allows for the identification of new sources detected by Swift-XRT, but not by XMM-NEWTON and ROSAT, and vice versa. As a result, a comprehensive, real-time monitoring service has been created that combines data from multiple missions.

We explore the ground state characteristics of the $t$-$J$ model on a triangular lattice with a combination of nearest neighbor and next-nearest neighbor hoppings. By employing the density matrix renormalization group method, we investigate the phase diagram and compare it to the conventional $t$-$J$ model. The phase diagram consists of three distinct regimes: a plaquette valence bond phase, a N\'eel magnetic ordered phase, and a stripy magnetic ordered phase. Notably, the plaquette phase exhibits significant dimerization, distinguishing it from the N\'eel and stripy phases. The weights of the dimerization within the plaquette phase show a strong correlation with the weights of the next-nearest neighbor hoppings. The weights of the plaquette phase show a strong correlation with the weights of the next-nearest neighbor hoppings. The phase diagram consists of a tricritical point, a first-order phase transition between the N\'eel and stripy phases, and a phase boundary separating the plaquette and stripy phases.

This research develops a new method for identifying the most influential global trade networks that can withstand various economic disruptions. The model incorporates a dynamic factor model to pinpoint the impact of large-scale economic shocks, and it uses the Generalized Extreme Value model to model the uncertainty in shock identification. The proposed method is applied to the global trade network, and the results show that the 2008 financial crisis had a significant effect on trade between countries. In contrast, the impact of regional economic disruptions is mostly confined to specific regional trade networks. The analysis also reveals that economic growth in developed countries tends to have a positive effect on trade, whereas economic growth in developing countries has a limited impact. In contrast, the identification of large-scale economic disruptions in developed countries has a significant effect on trade, whereas regional economic disruptions in developing countries have a limited effect.

Poisson gauge theories emerge as the noncommutative extension of certain classical mechanical systems. These theories, characterized by Poisson brackets instead of commutators, have a natural classical counterpart and are semi-classical equivalents of noncommutative gauge theories. This study focuses on Poisson sigma models, a specific class of Poisson gauge theories, examining their properties and finding a connection with the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism. By exploiting this connection, the paper investigates the constraints imposed by the gauge symmetry on the fields and presents a general solution through the use of free fields. This work also generalizes the Palatini action in the context of Poisson sigma models, leading to a novel application in Poisson gauge theories.

We've developed a novel approach to designing and building passive linear quantum systems, such as filters, by drawing inspiration from the H infinity method used in traditional control systems, but with a quantum twist. This approach allows us to solve a wide range of problems related to optimal system design and operations, while also providing robust solutions to systems vulnerable to disturbances. By applying this method, we can achieve the best possible outcomes, even in uncertain conditions, without the need for additional assumptions. Importantly, our method can be used to solve these problems in a computationally efficient manner. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we've applied it to a specific example of a quantum filter, showing how it can be used to optimize the design of a physical filter in a wide range of operating conditions.

Accurate time perception, which is crucial for cognitive processing, remains somewhat elusive to fully understand. Research has consistently shown that animals and humans have a remarkable capacity for estimating time intervals both objectively and subjectively. While some studies have found that animals rely on internal biological processes, such as respiration and pupil size, to gauge time, humans tend to use more complex cognitive methods. Our study aimed to investigate and compare the effectiveness of different biological measures, including respiration, heart rate, skin conductance, electroencephalogram, and EEG, in tracking perceived time in humans. Our findings indicate that all the measured variables can provide a reliable indication of the passage of time, which can be as short as 10 seconds, and that the brain's alpha wave patterns in the EEG are particularly consistent in their correlation with subjective time perception.

Decision-making is a fundamental aspect of life. When faced with a choice between two options, we often struggle to choose, and the time it takes to make a decision can be influenced by factors like the attractiveness of the options and the level of uncertainty surrounding the outcome. This process can be modeled as a dynamic process involving search and exploration, and our research involves analyzing the probability density of the decision-making time using the drift-diffusion model. By applying Brownian motion, we derive a differential equation governing the decision-making process, allowing us to study the properties of the decision-time distribution. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the probability of selecting one option over another is linked to the individual's decision policy. Building upon this, we extend our model to incorporate a more complex feature by means of an ordinary differential equation, and utilize numerical methods to validate our results.

The machine learning fairness community is driven by a sense of purpose to create
fair algorithms to bridge the gap between moral and legal principles and technical
implementations. However, the gap between our technical and legal language is
significant, particularly in the US, where our concepts often don't align with the
legal terms used in court rulings. This mismatch can lead to uncertainty about
how to translate our technical findings into actionable legal insights. To tackle
this challenge, we've developed a new research approach: examining the tensions
between our technical and legal language through close readings of relevant US
court decisions. This project aims to contribute to a more informed, legally
conscious ML fairness community.

A novel approach to detecting neutrinos utilizes magnetization linked to the radiative emission of neutrino pairs, which can occur within a magnetized plasma. This mechanism is explored in detail within a magnetized plasma, considering both the resonance and non-resonance regimes. The associated probability of neutrino pair emission is derived, and the resulting magnetic field distribution is calculated over a broad frequency spectrum. This method can potentially be employed to measure the Earth's core temperature and magnetic field by observing the resulting neutrino flux.

The observed splittings in A=7 to 8 hypernuclei multiplets, resulting from charge symmetry breaking, are found to be significantly smaller than those in A=5 to 6 hyperfragments. This outcome is attributed to the enhanced role of central and tensor couplings in the effective density and gradient of the $\pi$ and $K$ condensations at lower isospin values.

Online platforms like social media can use algorithms to predict users' behaviors based on their past actions, such as watching videos or interacting with content. These predictive models can then influence what content is shown next, often without users even realizing it. Our research focuses on how these models can be deceived by intentionally manipulating other users' behaviors, such as liking videos in bulk, to skew profiling accuracy. We've developed a game-theoretic framework that allows us to analyze and compare the effectiveness of different deception strategies, such as group manipulation or gradual, long-term influence operations, to outperform other approaches. Our findings show that these deceptive methods can significantly reduce the accuracy of profiling algorithms, up to 80% in some cases, and offer valuable insights into how to detect and prevent such manipulative tactics in the future.

In this context, we investigate the coalescent process resulting from the division of a random set of elements, $U$, which contains unique items with elements selected independently at random. The size of each offspring in this set is determined by a random variable, $Z$, with elements selected independently at random. By establishing a connection between the coalescent process and a random variable, $X$, that represents the number of generations it takes for a family tree to form, we derive an explicit formula for the distribution of $X$. Our analysis reveals that the characteristics of $U$ and $Z$ have a significant influence on the independence properties of the coalescent process. When $U$ is a binary random variable and $Z$ follows a specific distribution, the coalescent process is found to be independent. However, when $U$ is not binary and $Z$ follows a different distribution, the coalscence times exhibit strong correlation. Our findings are further supported by numerical simulations.

We develop a formula for determining the specific characteristics of a measure for a hard core model with a countable set of distinct interaction parameters on a Cayley tree, where the measure can be uniquely defined for any given configuration of interaction parameters. This result is notable due to an earlier finding that, in the case of a countable set of parameters, certain configurations could give rise to non-uniquely defined measures.

We have compiled a comprehensive catalog of stellar kinematics in the Milky Way's central region using the LAMOST and APOGEE surveys. We analyzed proper motion data from LAMOST to identify the center of the Milky Way and divided the surrounding area into a grid. We then extracted stellar samples from this grid and applied the Schwarzschild model to estimate the stellar motion. We compared our results to those obtained by other studies, including the OSA project, the Geneva-CRAnton survey, and the VVV survey. We found that our LAMOST-APOGEE data provided the most accurate estimate of the Milky Way's central motion, with the OSA project being the second most accurate. We also found that our LAMOST-APOGOGEE data were in agreement with the VVV survey, but the Geneva-CRAnton survey was inconsistent. We also found that our LAMOST-APOGEE data were in agreement with the LAMOST-APOGEE data, but the OSA project was inconsistent. We also found that our LAMOST-APOGEE data were in agreement with the LAMOST-APOGOGEE data, but the OSA project was inconsistent. We also found that our LAMOST-APOGEE data were in agreement with the LAMOST-APOGOGEE data, but the OSA project was inconsistent.

In relativistic coupled-cluster theory, the analytic energy derivative approach offers significant improvements over existing methods. By leveraging this approach, we derived first and second-order first-order properties such as atomic isotope shifts and hyperfine constants. Through a detailed analysis of the first and second-order first-order first derivatives of the total energy, we established a method for efficiently and accurately calculating these properties. When applied to various closed-shell atoms, our results demonstrated the method's effectiveness and achieved good agreement with experimental results for atomic hydrogen isotope shifts. Additionally, we calculated and compared the results for atomic and ionic hyperfine constants, highlighting the method's potential for high accuracy and its capacity to handle complex multiconfiguration interacting Hamiltonians.
